name: Absorb LMS
parent: Absorb Software Inc. (Welsh, Carson, Anderson & Stowe)
toolCategory: Horizontal corporate LMS

verdict.line: Absorb sells the container, not the contents — it competes for the LMS line item, and every multifamily course inside it still has to be bought, built and re-written by someone on the customer's payroll.
verdict.doInstead: Do not argue platform features. Ask who writes the fair housing course, who updates it when a state changes its rules, and what that headcount costs; then price PerformanceHQ against the platform fee plus that internal content burden. If they are already locked into Absorb, position Grace Hill content delivered into it rather than a rip-and-replace.

ownership.value: Majority-owned by Welsh, Carson, Anderson & Stowe (WCAS Fund XIII); acquired from Silversmith Capital Partners in 2021

pricing.value: Not published on the vendor site; quote-only.

positioning.value: "The AI-powered LMS that actually knows your business" / "The Industry's #1 Learning Management System" — a horizontal enterprise LMS marketed on platform capability rather than any industry vertical.

strengths.text: WCAS reports Absorb serves approximately 28 million users across 1,700 clients in 34 countries.
Publishes 20,000+ pre-built courses through its Absorb Amplify content portfolio and pre-built connectors to ADP, Workday, Salesforce and 40+ other systems.
Absorb Create offers AI-assisted course generation with quizzes, video, translations and voice-over.

gaps.text: Absorb's public site names Sony, Gap, Johnson & Johnson, Samsung and Toyota and cites healthcare, financial services and manufacturing — it publishes no multifamily or property-management vertical.
Absorb's content story is a general business catalog (Amplify) plus customer-authored courses; no fair housing, state-specific landlord-tenant or CAM/CAPS/CALP credential content is published.

whyWeWin: Grace Hill maintains the multifamily course library itself — the customer does not staff a content team to keep fair housing current.
Fair housing and state-specific compliance content ships with the product, not as a project.
Role- and property-based assignment maps to how a portfolio is actually organized, not just to HR job codes.
askThis: Who on your team writes and owns the fair housing course today, and when was it last reviewed?
When a state changes a compliance requirement, how long until your courses reflect it — and who does that work?
How many of the 20,000 courses in the library are about running an apartment community?

objections.objection: We already have Absorb enterprise-wide.
objections.response: Then the platform question is settled. The open question is what goes in it for site teams — ask what happens when a fair housing rule changes and who is on the hook to update the course.

doNotSay: Do not say Absorb has no compliance content — it publishes a general business and compliance catalog; the verifiable point is that it publishes no multifamily-specific library.
Do not quote an Absorb price. None is published.

tr-multifamily-content.note: Publishes no multifamily or property-management vertical library; industries cited are healthcare, financial services and manufacturing.

tr-vendor-maintained.note: Amplify library content is licensed from third-party publishers; customer-authored courses are maintained by the customer.

tr-fair-housing.note: No fair housing course is identified in published Amplify materials; the third-party catalog is not fully enumerated publicly.

tr-state-specific.note: No US state-specific compliance variants documented publicly.

name: Adobe Learning Manager
toolCategory: Horizontal enterprise LMS inside a marketing-technology suite

verdict.line: Adobe Learning Manager is bought by companies already standardized on Adobe Experience Cloud to train customers, partners and franchisees — it is a brand-experience learning tool, not a property-compliance system, and it should not be on a multifamily training shortlist.
verdict.doInstead: If it surfaces, it is almost always because corporate marketing or a franchise/partner program already owns it. Do not pitch against it — scope Grace Hill to the onsite compliance and role-based training it was never bought to do, and let the two coexist.

ownership.value: Adobe Inc. (Nasdaq: ADBE) — marketed under Adobe Experience Cloud

pricing.value: Not published on the product page; quote-only through Adobe sales.

positioning.value: "Personalize learning for your customers, partners, and employees" with "adaptive, AI-driven experiences" and "powerful automations and workflows."

strengths.text: Explicitly serves three audiences — employees, customers, and partners/franchisees — making it strong for extended-enterprise and brand-consistent training.
Deep native integration with Adobe Experience Manager Sites, Marketo Engage, Adobe Commerce, Adobe Connect, Microsoft Teams and Salesforce.
Supports online, instructor-led, virtual instructor-led and blended delivery plus multilingual certification programs.

gaps.text: Adobe positions Learning Manager as a delivery platform, not an authoring tool — Adobe recommends buying Adobe Captivate separately to create interactive content.
No industry vertical content library is offered; the product page names no multifamily, real estate or housing-compliance content.

whyWeWin: Grace Hill is bought to reduce fair housing and compliance exposure at the property level, which is not the job Adobe Learning Manager is sold to do.
The multifamily course library and its upkeep come with the subscription rather than requiring a separate authoring tool and an internal instructional designer.
askThis: Is Learning Manager owned by marketing for brand and partner programs, or by HR for onsite compliance?
Who builds the courses today — and are you also paying for Adobe Captivate to do it?

objections.objection: We're an Adobe shop; we'll just use Learning Manager.
objections.response: That is a sensible place for customer and partner enablement. The gap is the content: Adobe positions ALM as a delivery platform and points to Captivate for authoring, so the fair housing and state compliance courses still need a source.

doNotSay: Do not claim Adobe Learning Manager cannot do compliance training — Adobe names compliance among employee use cases.
Do not quote an Adobe Learning Manager price.

name: AirMason
toolCategory: Employee handbook tool

verdict.line: Real state-by-state content and attorney-reviewed updates — but it is an HR employment-law handbook, not the operations manual that governs how a leasing office runs.

hq.value: Not published on the vendor's about page

founded.value: Not published on the vendor's about page

ownership.value: Not disclosed on the vendor site

size.value: Not published

pricing.value: Published. Startup (1-99 employees) $999/year or $149/mo billed monthly; Small Business (100-199 employees) $1,499/year or $199/mo billed monthly; Enterprise (200+) custom pricing.

positioning.value: Positions itself as helping organizations "build culture-driven employee handbooks" while streamlining employment law compliance.

strengths.text: Ships real prewritten content — a library of expert-curated handbook and policy templates rather than an empty builder.

State-specific compliance content covering all 50 states, with AI-powered employment law monitoring and attorney review driving automated compliance updates. This is genuine vendor-maintained regulatory currency in its domain.
E-signature collection with audit trails and signature tracking, plus version control and real-time editing.
AirAssist, an AI assistant that answers employee policy questions, plus HRIS/SSO integrations with Workday, BambooHR and ADP.
Published pricing with a low entry point — $999/year for organizations under 100 employees — which makes it easy for a small operator to say yes.

gaps.text: AirMason's content domain is employment law and the employee handbook. Its site does not describe multifamily operations policy content — fair housing, leasing, tax credit compliance, maintenance or emergency procedures.
The state-specific content and compliance monitoring described are employment law focused, not landlord-tenant or housing regulation.
Position-based policy assignment and linkage to a training course library are not described in AirMason's public product materials.

whyWeWin: Two different documents. AirMason handles the HR handbook. Grace Hill handles the operations manual — over a thousand multifamily policies, forms and job descriptions across 18+ manuals covering emergency procedures, leasing, tax credit compliance, maintenance and operations.

Their regulatory watch is employment law. Ours is multifamily: fair housing, HUD guidance, housing compliance. Neither substitutes for the other, and only one of them governs what happens in the leasing office.
Grace Hill links policy to multifamily training in PerformanceHQ — the acknowledgment and the course that teaches the behavior report together.
Automatic assignment by location, position, group or employee matches a portfolio structure that an HR-centric handbook tool is not designed around.
askThis: Their state content tracks employment law. Who is tracking fair housing and landlord-tenant changes for your property teams?
Does your handbook tell a leasing consultant how to handle a reasonable accommodation request, or is that in a different document entirely?
How do you assign a policy to just your maintenance techs at three properties in one state?
When someone acknowledges a policy, does that connect to any training that teaches them how to actually do it?
If a fair housing claim landed tomorrow, which system holds the proof, and does it cover the operations policy or just the handbook?

objections.objection: AirMason is much cheaper — $999 a year.
objections.response: It is, and for an HR handbook that may be exactly right. Just be clear on what you're buying. That price covers your employee handbook and employment-law updates. It does not cover the fair housing, leasing and tax-credit manuals your property teams actually work from. Those are the ones that show up in a complaint.

objections.objection: They already do state-specific content and attorney review.
objections.response: For employment law, yes, and that's real. But your exposure isn't only employment law. It's fair housing and housing compliance, and that's a completely different body of regulation. Ask them what their state content says about a reasonable accommodation request.

doNotSay: Do not say AirMason has no prewritten content or no state-specific content — it markets both, across all 50 states, with attorney review. Denying it is factually wrong and easy to disprove.
Do not state AirMason's ownership or headquarters — neither is published.
Do not claim their pricing is higher than ours or make any comparative price claim without approval.

po-prewritten-library.note: Pre-built, expert-curated handbook and policy templates. Content domain is HR/employment law, not multifamily operations.

po-regulatory-updates.note: AI-powered employment law monitoring with attorney review drives automated compliance updates — vendor-maintained, but scoped to employment law.

po-jurisdiction-variants.note: Content tailored to individual state requirements across all 50 states, in the employment law domain.

po-version-control.note: Real-time editing with document version management.

po-attestation.note: Electronic signature collection with audit trails and signature tracking.

po-esignature.note: E-signature management is a core marketed feature.

po-overdue-reporting.note: Signature tracking plus viewership and engagement analytics; dedicated overdue/exception reporting is not detailed.

po-position-assignment.note: Not described in public product materials.

po-content-search.note: AirAssist AI assistant answers employee policy questions, which implies reading policy content; a conventional full-text search feature is not described separately.

po-training-linkage.note: Not described in public product materials.

name: AktivBo
toolCategory: European real estate resident and commercial tenant survey and benchmarking firm

verdict.line: The one vendor in this set with a benchmark that rivals ours on disclosed scale — but it is Nordic and European in footprint, so compete on U.S. multifamily relevance and the remediation path, not on data volume.

hq.value: Stockholm, Sweden (Engelbrektsgatan 6, 114 32 Stockholm); also operates from Hamburg, Germany

ownership.value: Unknown — ownership structure not disclosed on public pages

size.value: Unknown — headcount not disclosed. Client base stated as over 450 housing and property companies across more than 20 countries.

pricing.value: Not published. Site directs to demo requests and contact.

positioning.value: A data-driven knowledge and platform company for the real estate industry, built on a "Measure, Analyze, and Act" model with continuous customer journey follow-up and benchmarking.

strengths.text: Large, explicitly disclosed benchmark: over 150 million responses in the database, 450+ real estate companies, 30+ years of industry experience, across more than 20 countries.

Covers both residential and commercial in one benchmark: CSC Residential, Moving in/out, New Production and Reconstruction on the residential side; CSC Commercial and Acquisition on the commercial side, spanning office, retail, restaurant, industrial, logistics and schools.
ESG and GRESB alignment: explicitly frames tenant engagement programs and tenant satisfaction improvement as scored components of the GRESB Real Estate Assessment.
Publishes benchmark response-rate transparency — a 63.1% average response rate for aggregated data across all companies in the Sweden benchmark 2023.
Supports regulatory survey standards including UK Tenant Satisfaction Measures (TSM), plus NPS and CES, with AI-powered text analysis and ERP/CRM API integration for trigger-based surveys.

gaps.text: Footprint and benchmark are European. Offices are disclosed in Stockholm and Hamburg, and the published benchmark reference point is the "Sweden benchmark 2023"; no U.S. office or U.S. multifamily benchmark is disclosed.
The published survey portfolio covers residential and commercial tenants plus change-management support; no employee engagement survey product is listed.
No commercial-real-estate-specific benchmark scale is disclosed on the CRE page — the 150 million figure is presented at the company level.
No pricing is published.
No training/LMS, policy management or mystery shopping product is offered.

whyWeWin: U.S. relevance: Kingsley benchmarks U.S. multifamily and commercial real estate operators; AktivBo's disclosed reference benchmark is Swedish and European.
Employee listening included: Grace Hill covers employee surveys alongside resident and CRE tenant; AktivBo's published line does not.
Closed loop into training, policy and mystery shop verification.
One U.S.-based vendor with U.S. fair housing and compliance context built in.
askThis: AktivBo's disclosed benchmark reference is the Sweden benchmark. Which peer set would your U.S. assets be compared against?
Do you also need employee engagement measured, and where does that sit today?
Who supports you day to day, and in which time zone?
Does your investor reporting need U.S. multifamily comparables, or is GRESB the driver?
After a tenant satisfaction finding, what is the path to training and verification onsite?

objections.objection: AktivBo has 150 million responses — that dwarfs your benchmark.
objections.response: It's a genuinely large dataset and we won't dispute it. It's also predominantly European, anchored on their published Sweden benchmark. A U.S. regional manager needs to be compared to U.S. operators, and they need the employee side too.

objections.objection: They handle both residential and commercial in one benchmark.
objections.response: So do we — plus employees, plus the ability to turn the finding into assigned training and a verification shop.

doNotSay: Do not dispute AktivBo's disclosed scale (150 million responses, 450+ companies, 30+ years, 20+ countries). It is published on their own site and easily checked.
Do not claim they cannot operate in the U.S. — say that no U.S. office or U.S. benchmark is disclosed publicly.
Do not quote an AktivBo price or headcount — neither is published.
Do not assert their data is not comparable without framing it as a question about which peer set applies.

sv-employee.note: Change management support is mentioned; no employee engagement survey product is listed.

sv-benchmark-dataset.note: Benchmarking is a core product across residential and commercial real estate.

Response-rate transparency published as a 63.1% average for aggregated data across all companies in the Sweden benchmark 2023. No separate U.S. or CRE-specific scale is disclosed.

sv-portfolio-rollup.note: Asset-management-level analysis and portfolio views are offered alongside property-level results.

sv-lifecycle.note: Continuous customer journey follow-up with API integration to ERP/CRM for automated trigger-based surveys; move-in/move-out and acquisition surveys.

name: ALN Apartment Data
toolCategory: Market rent comparables data

verdict.line: The long-standing phone-survey house — 195,000+ properties contacted on a roughly monthly rotation — so compete on refresh speed and on coverage of properties that don't answer the call.

founded.value: 1991, in Dallas, Texas

ownership.value: Private

size.value: Unknown — operates research call centers in Dallas/Fort Worth, Texas and Mayfield, Kentucky.

funding.value: Unknown

pricing.value: Not published; the site directs to a demo request or sales contact.

positioning.value: Positions as nationwide multifamily data delivering 'accurate, reliable data on multifamily properties such as occupancy, market and effective rents, concessions, amenities, historical data, new construction, and much more', built on a verified primary-research call-center model.

strengths.text: Published coverage: over 195,000 properties, more than 25.8 million units and 11,800+ management companies, across all 50 states.
Primary research through owned call centers in Dallas/Fort Worth, Texas and Mayfield, Kentucky, with proprietary data checks on each completed survey.

Multi-channel collection: call-center surveys, publicly accessible sources (corporate websites, job listings, news outlets), direct feeds from owners and management companies, and third-party sources for new construction.
Explicitly tracks concessions and effective rents alongside occupancy, amenities and new construction, with historical data; founded 1991, giving long time series.

gaps.text: Property-level data is refreshed by contact 'every 25 business days'; semi-static attributes such as amenities and lease terms follow a quarterly and annual rotation. Only new construction is described as updating daily.
ALN prioritizes updating conventional multifamily properties with 50 or more units, so update emphasis falls on larger stabilised conventional properties rather than smaller or specialty housing.
API access is not described on the site pages reviewed; products listed are ALN OnLine, Vendor Edge Pro, Compass and Locator.
Pricing is not published.

whyWeWin: A roughly monthly contact cycle and a daily automated feed answer different questions — make the buyer name how often they reprice.
HelloData®'s comp and concession data comes without depending on a comp's onsite team picking up the phone.
askThis: How often do you reprice, and how often does your comp data actually refresh underneath that?
What happens when a comp stops taking the survey call?
How is coverage in your submarkets for properties under 50 units?
Is there an API, or is this ALN OnLine and exports?

objections.objection: ALN data is verified by a human, so it's more reliable.
objections.response: Human verification is a genuine strength on the properties they reach. The trade-off is cadence — every 25 business days for property-level data — and coverage on comps that don't participate.

doNotSay: Do not say ALN data is inaccurate — their methodology page documents verification checks.
Do not state ALN has no API — say it is not described on their public pages.
Do not quote an ALN price; none is published.

Implementation services from $750.

positioning.value: "A culture-first online employee handbook and policy management platform for HR teams" — positioned against static PDF handbooks.

strengths.text: Published, transparent pricing — one of the few vendors in this set a buyer can price without a sales call.

Regulatory currency is priced as a separate add-on — Labor Law Change Updates start at $49/month and vary by state — rather than being included in the base subscription.

whyWeWin: Blissbook keeps your handbook current. Grace Hill keeps your operating manual current. Their regulatory watch is labor law. Ours is multifamily housing regulation. The complaint that ends up in front of your counsel is far more likely to be fair housing than an employment handbook clause.
Grace Hill's content maintenance is part of the product, not a per-state add-on line item.
Policy connects to multifamily training in PerformanceHQ, and assignment runs by location, position, group or employee — the way a portfolio is organized.

name: CEL & Associates
toolCategory: Real estate consulting firm with a satisfaction survey practice

verdict.line: A consulting firm that runs surveys, not a survey platform — strong on custom reporting and executive analysis, but they publish no benchmark scale and there is no software, no lifecycle automation and no remediation path.

founded.value: Unknown — founding year not disclosed on public pages

ownership.value: Unknown — ownership not disclosed on public pages

size.value: Unknown — headcount not disclosed

pricing.value: Not published. Engagement-based consulting model; no rate card disclosed.

positioning.value: A real estate consulting firm whose stated mission is to "optimize enterprise value, improve your company's NOI and give you the competitive edge," offering strategy consulting, satisfaction surveys and compensation benchmarking.

strengths.text: Covers four respondent types under one firm: resident, tenant, employee and client satisfaction surveys, plus custom surveys.

Deep, consultant-produced reporting: executive summaries prepared by senior associates, Service Gap Analysis identifying lost potential, portfolio overviews with alert status indicators, and Score Watch dashboards tracking up to 5 years of trending data.
The REACT R process includes an action plan and guidance for completion, so the deliverable is not just a score.
Measures three satisfaction indices and nine critical business success factors, with reporting deliberately matched to "the reporting level that matches their internal abilities to manage data."
Established adjacent credibility in real estate compensation benchmarking through the RCLCO-CEL Real Estate Compensation & Benefits Survey.

gaps.text: Benchmark scale and history are not disclosed. The resident survey page refers only to "comparative scores from CEL's extensive database of survey data" with no respondent count, company count or number of years.
The offering is a consulting engagement producing reports, not a self-serve platform; no software product, dashboard login or API is described on the survey pages.
No event-triggered lifecycle survey program is described — the described model is periodic survey engagements with trending over up to 5 years.
No training/LMS, policy management or mystery shopping product is offered.
Founding year, ownership and headcount are not disclosed publicly.

whyWeWin: A disclosed benchmark: the Kingsley Index™ publishes its multifamily and CRE scale and history; CEL describes an 'extensive database' without stating what is in it.
Continuous listening instead of a periodic engagement — event-triggered surveys catch problems in the week they happen, not at the next study.
Software plus service: dashboards your regionals use themselves, not a report that lands with the executive team.
The finding routes into assigned training, a policy update and a verification shop.
askThis: When CEL shows you a comparative score, how many responses and how many companies is that comparison built from, and over how many years?
How often do you get results — once a study, or continuously?
Can a property manager log in and see their own numbers, or do they wait for the report?
How much of the value is the consultant's interpretation versus data your team can act on directly?
After the action plan is written, who verifies it was executed at the property?

objections.objection: CEL gives us a senior consultant who writes the executive summary.
objections.response: That's real value and we'd never dismiss it. The question is whether the comparative score behind it is one you can size. Ask them what's in the database — we publish ours.

objections.objection: We only need a survey once a year.
objections.response: That's the periodic model, and it means an issue that starts in February isn't visible until the next study. Event-triggered listening changes when you find out.

doNotSay: Do not claim CEL's database is small or inadequate. It is simply undisclosed — say that, and ask the question.
Do not state a CEL founding year, headcount, client count or price. None are published.
Do not disparage the consulting model — for some buyers the senior-analyst deliverable is precisely what they want.
Do not claim they don't do employee or commercial tenant surveys — both are in their published service list.

Score Watch dashboards track up to 5 years of trending for a client's own data — that is client trend depth, not benchmark scale. This is a finding.

verdict.line: Coursebox is a self-serve AI authoring tool that turns a customer's own documents into courses — it is the do-it-yourself alternative to buying a library, which means it only wins when the buyer has already decided to write their own fair housing content.
verdict.doInstead: Do not battlecard it. Treat its appearance as a diagnostic: someone is planning to build compliance content in-house. whyWeWin: Grace Hill supplies a maintained multifamily curriculum; Coursebox supplies a tool for writing your own.

verdict.line: A credible employee engagement platform with a transparently documented benchmark methodology — but it is HR-side only, with no resident or commercial tenant surveys and no multifamily operator benchmark.

founded.value: 2009, by Didier Elzinga, Doug English, Rod Hamilton and Jon Williams

ownership.value: Private, venture-backed; Certified B Corporation

size.value: Unknown — headcount not verified from a primary source. Customer base reported as more than 25 million employees across 6,500+ companies.

funding.value: $150 million Series F (July 2021) led by Sequoia Capital China and TDM Growth Partners, at a $1.5 billion valuation

pricing.value: Unknown — no published rate card verified from a Culture Amp primary source.

positioning.value: An employee experience platform combining engagement surveys, performance and development, with benchmark insights refreshed twice a year.

strengths.text: Unusually transparent benchmark methodology: industry and geography benchmarks require a minimum of 20 companies and 20,000 people, with at least 10 employees responding from each company.

Benchmarks refresh on a stated cadence — new benchmark sets twice a year, in January and July, using responses collected 1 July of the previous year through 30 June of the current year, counting each company only once.
Large aggregate customer base: reported as more than 25 million employees across 6,500+ companies.
Discloses an average survey response rate "well over 80%" across its benchmark data.
Well-capitalized: $150M Series F at a $1.5B valuation in July 2021.

gaps.text: Culture Amp's published product line is employee experience only — engagement, performance and development. No resident survey or commercial tenant survey product is offered.
Benchmark cuts are by industry and geography with a 20-company / 20,000-person minimum; no multifamily or real estate operator benchmark is disclosed.
Benchmark data refreshes only twice a year (January and July), so a mid-cycle comparison is against a dataset up to six months old.
No training/LMS with multifamily compliance content, no policy management and no mystery shopping product, so a finding cannot be routed to verified remediation.

whyWeWin: One vendor for residents, employees and commercial tenants; Culture Amp covers only employees.
Benchmark relevance: Kingsley compares a property operator to property operators, not to a cross-industry cut.
Property, region and portfolio rollups are native for us; an HR platform is organized around org charts, not asset hierarchies.
A survey finding becomes an assigned course, a policy update and a verification shop.
askThis: Culture Amp benchmarks by industry and geography with a 20-company minimum. Which cut are your properties actually compared against?
Where does resident feedback live today, and who reconciles it against the employee data?
Can you see results rolled up by property and region, or only by reporting line?
Your benchmark refreshes in January and July. Does that cadence work for how you run the portfolio?
After an engagement finding, what is the path to assigned training and to proving it worked?

objections.objection: HR already owns Culture Amp and likes it.
objections.response: Then leave it where it works. The gap is on the resident and commercial tenant side, and on comparing your onsite teams to other property operators rather than a cross-industry cut.

objections.objection: Their benchmark methodology is well documented.
objections.response: It genuinely is — 20 companies and 20,000 people minimum, refreshed twice a year. Just check which cut your properties land in. Industry-and-geography is not the same as multifamily operator.

doNotSay: Do not claim Culture Amp has no benchmark or a weak one. Their documented minimums (20 companies / 20,000 people) and twice-yearly refresh are public and defensible.
Do not quote a Culture Amp price — no primary-source rate card was verified.
Do not state a Culture Amp headcount — it is not verified.
Do not claim they are losing customers or in decline — no public source supports it.
Do not say they 'can't' survey residents — say that no resident or CRE tenant product appears in their published line.

AI-powered employee search using plain language queries — staff ask a question rather than hunting for a document title.
Real-time dashboards and customizable reporting on policy status, adoption and gaps.
Enterprise scale and credibility — 25,000 customers, 2,000+ employees, and reference logos including Mastercard, Barclays, General Mills and Heineken.

whyWeWin: Diligent sells governance machinery to a general counsel. Grace Hill sells the multifamily operating manual to the person who runs properties — over a thousand policies, forms and job descriptions across 18+ manuals, already written.

Our policies link to multifamily training in PerformanceHQ so acknowledgment and instruction sit in one report.
Assignment by location, position, group or employee is built for property portfolios rather than corporate departments.

Do not assert that Diligent has no prewritten content. The accurate statement is that a content library is not described on the Policy Manager page. Ask the question.

verdict.doInstead: Concede the platform, then move to content. Ask what the plan and budget are for the industry-specific content their site teams actually need — leasing, maintenance, and the compliance areas that carry risk.

verdict.line: A new, founder-led shop provider selling multifamily credibility rather than scale — it competes on who reads the report, so the contest is coverage, comparability and what happens after the shop.

stackLayer.name: Resolution · The Resolution Layer for Multifamily
stackLayer.note: Competes for the resolution layer position, or for one slice of it.

founded.value: Not published. Surfaced in the Grace Hill competitive channel on 17 July 2026 as a new company.

ownership.value: Founder-owned. Eric Franco, Founder & Director of Training.

size.value: Unknown — no team page, shopper network size or coverage map is published.

funding.value: Unknown

pricing.value: Not published. Customized scoring criteria are stated as included at no additional cost.

positioning.value: Positions itself as going beyond scoring — it 'connects evaluation findings to coaching, training, and measurable results' to help teams 'convert more prospects into residents'. Serves multifamily residential exclusively.

strengths.text: Founder brings 20+ years in multifamily, from leasing agent to regional leadership, including systems training and performance improvement — credibility with the buyer is his core asset.
Multifamily-exclusive. No retail or restaurant business diluting the rubric.
Eight shop types published, including new-construction lease-up shops and competitive shops — a wider published menu than most new entrants.
Customized scoring criteria included with every shop at no additional cost — removes the setup-fee objection a buyer may have hit elsewhere.
Every evaluation ships with a 13-page report, a 'Leasing Decision Journey' framework and a 30-day improvement blueprint.
Offers a Follow-Up Shop roughly 30 days after the evaluation, explicitly to measure whether coaching changed behavior — a closed loop most shop vendors do not sell.

gaps.text: No shopper network size, geographic coverage or capacity is published anywhere on the site — the practical question for a multi-state portfolio is unanswered.
No named clients, testimonials or case studies are published.
No industry benchmark dataset is described — scoring is customized per client, which by design makes results comparable within an account but not against the wider industry.
No pricing, turnaround time, or shopper recruitment method is published.
No third-party coverage, trade press, review-site presence or funding record could be found in an August 2026 search — the only public footprint is the company's own site.

whyWeWin: Benchmarking. Customized scoring is a real selling point for them and the exact thing that prevents an industry comparison — ask what a score of 87 means against anyone but themselves.

Scale and continuity. Ellis and EPMS are Grace Hill companies with decades of shopping behind them; a founder-led firm's capacity and coverage across a multi-state portfolio is an open question worth asking about plainly.

The loop is already built. Their follow-up shop measures whether coaching landed; ours routes a low score into an assigned course and re-measures inside the same platform, with no second vendor and no manual handoff.
One contract. A buyer comparing shops alone is comparing one line item — shops sitting next to training, policy, surveys and reputation is a different purchase.
askThis: How many shoppers do you have in the markets where my properties actually are, and what's your monthly capacity across the portfolio?
If my scoring criteria are custom to me, what do I compare my results against outside my own portfolio?
Who does the work if you're unavailable for a month — what's the bench?
When a shop comes back low, what actually assigns the training and proves the score moved?
doNotSay: Do not disparage the founder or imply a small firm can't deliver a good shop. Twenty years of multifamily operations is real credibility and the buyer may know him personally — attacking it will cost you the room.
Do not claim they can't do video, lease-up or competitive shops. All eight shop types are published on their site.
Do not quote or guess their pricing. None is published.
Do not present the absence of named clients as proof they have none — it is an absence of public evidence, and say it that way.

whenItComesUp.why: A new entrant selling operator credibility rather than infrastructure. It competes for the shop line item, and it will be attractive to a buyer who has been burned by a big vendor's generic rubric. The open questions are capacity, comparability and continuity — not competence.
whenItComesUp.say: If you know Eric, that experience is worth something — a shop report written by someone who has actually run a region reads differently, and I wouldn't argue with that. The questions I'd want answered are practical: coverage in your markets, what you benchmark the score against, and what happens after the report lands.
whenItComesUp.avoid: Don't attack the founder or the size of the business. It reads as threatened, and if the buyer has a relationship with him you've lost the conversation rather than the deal.
whenItComesUp.redirect: When a shop comes back low, what happens next in your world — who gets told, what training gets assigned, and how do you know it improved?

Ask him those three, then ask us.

name: EliseAI
toolCategory: AI leasing agent

verdict.line: A Grace Hill partner in three programs and a competitor on one product. Their training content ships inside PerformanceHQ and their data flows into ours — both reasons to buy. SentimentAI overlaps our Surveys line, and that part is a deal you compete in like any other.
verdict.doInstead: Say the partnership out loud first — a prospect running EliseAI will find out anyway, and hearing it from you is worth more than the thirty seconds it costs. Grace Hill and EliseAI co-published a September 2025 report analyzing EliseAI's impact on resident NPS using Grace Hill survey data. Then compete on the one thing that actually overlaps: where a prospect is weighing SentimentAI against Grace Hill Surveys, compete on scope, the benchmark set behind the score, and what happens after the score exists. Stay factual and sourced, never disparage them, and never discuss the commercial terms of the relationship. Tell the partnership owner after the deal, not before — they should not be surprised by something they could have handled.

hq.value: New York, NY (401 Fifth Avenue), with office hubs in New York, San Francisco, Boston and Chicago

founded.value: Unknown

ownership.value: Private, venture-backed

size.value: Over 300 full-time employees as of the August 2025 Series E announcement, up from 150 a year earlier.

funding.value: $250M Series E announced August 16, 2025, led by Andreessen Horowitz with Bessemer Venture Partners, Sapphire Ventures and Navitas Capital; prior $75M Series D announced August 2024 at a valuation stated to exceed $1 billion.

pricing.value: Not published on the EliseAI website.

positioning.value: Positions as an end-to-end AI platform across the leasing-to-resident journey — EliseCRM, VoiceAI, prospect management, AI-guided tours, move-in, maintenance, renewals and delinquency — communicating by text, email, chat and voice across 51 written and 7 spoken languages, with a separate healthcare vertical.

strengths.text: Stated scale as of August 2025: over 600 owners and operators in housing, powering roughly 10% of the U.S. apartment market, with 75% of NMHC's Top 50 operators as customers and over $100 million in ARR.
Very well capitalized — $250M Series E led by a16z in August 2025, following a $75M Series D at a valuation stated above $1 billion.
Full lifecycle coverage from prospect to renewal and delinquency, including VoiceAI, lease audits and a maintenance app.
SentimentAI adds resident sentiment surveys triggered at renewals, maintenance completion and move-outs, with real-time dashboards and feedback embedded in the resident timeline.
Participates in Grace Hill's Training Partner Program, Survey Partner Program and Integration Partner list, and co-published a September 2025 report with Grace Hill.

gaps.text: The SentimentAI announcement describes dashboards and response tracking; competitive or industry benchmarking against an external dataset is not described.
The EliseAI homepage product listing does not include training, policy management, mystery shopping or reputation management.
Pricing is not published.

whyWeWin: This is a partner relationship, not a win column. The joint September 2025 report used Grace Hill survey data to measure EliseAI's impact on resident NPS — that is the story to tell.

Where scope does overlap, Grace Hill's survey line is built around a benchmarked industry dataset; EliseAI's SentimentAI is described around in-platform dashboards. State the difference factually and let the buyer decide.
askThis: Are you looking for resident sentiment inside your leasing platform, or a benchmarked survey program you can compare against the industry?
Who consumes the resident feedback — the onsite team in the moment, or asset management and ownership in a quarterly review?
Do you need the survey results to drive training or action planning, or just to be visible?
Have you seen the joint Grace Hill and EliseAI report on resident NPS? Would that be useful to your team?

objections.objection: We're already using EliseAI, so we get resident feedback there.
objections.response: That's great — and EliseAI is a Grace Hill partner; we co-published a report measuring their impact on resident NPS using Grace Hill survey data. The two work together. If you also need benchmarked survey results against the industry, that's the conversation to have.

objections.objection: Aren't you competing with EliseAI?
objections.response: We partner with them. EliseAI participates in our partner programs and we've published joint research. I'm not going to position against a partner — let me show you how the two fit together.

doNotSay: Never disparage EliseAI or characterize their product, service or company negatively. Compete on what we do better, sourced — not on what they do badly.
Never state, imply or speculate about any commercial terms of the Grace Hill / EliseAI relationship — revenue share, exclusivity, fees or anything else.
Do not claim EliseAI 'has no' surveys or benchmarking — SentimentAI exists; benchmarking against an external dataset is simply not described publicly.
Do not compete on their training content or the integration. Those ship inside our platform and are a reason to buy us, not a thing to argue with.

verdict.line: If the operator runs Dayforce, eloomi arrives already paid for — so the fight is never over whether they have a learning platform, it is over whether a curated general-business library from "top providers" is what a leasing office needs to stay out of a fair housing claim.

ownership.value: Private

positioning.value: Positions training as the way to maximize platform ROI — combining expert-led onboarding (in person, virtual and at HQ) with self-paced, compliance-focused content in one platform.

gaps.text: The offering is described as onboarding and upskilling teams on Entrata's Operations Experience Platform — the course library is product-focused rather than a broad multifamily operations curriculum.

whyWeWin: Entrata Academy is built to make people good at Entrata; Grace Hill is built to make people good at the job and provable in an audit — those are different products and can coexist.

positioning.value: Current site positions Escal8 as an AI-powered talent intelligence platform assessing employees across eight dimensions (skills, performance, growth, digital fluency, automation, capacity, culture, risk) to answer what to automate, who to develop and who to invest in. Content maintained by a vendor that has publicly repositioned away from the vertical carries currency risk — ask who is updating it.

name: Flair
toolCategory: AI conversation intelligence for leasing calls, with synthetic email shops

verdict.line: Flair reads every leasing call instead of sampling a few shops — it is a different product bought with the same budget, so it is a substitution risk, not a feature gap.
verdict.doInstead: Do not run this as a battlecard fight and do not try to win it by arguing shop quality — you will lose on volume math. Qualify what the buyer is actually trying to fix: if they want coverage of their own call volume, that is a product and strategy conversation, so log the deal and route it to product and strategy. Where the buyer also needs an unsolicited, unaffiliated prospect experience across onsite, video and email — which conversation intelligence of your own agents does not produce — position the two as complementary, not competing.

ownership.value: Private

size.value: 11–50 employees (vendor directory listing)

pricing.value: Not published; vendor directory requires a verified buyer account to view pricing. Public site offers free introductory secret shops.

positioning.value: "Flair is the conversation intelligence layer of the leasing tech stack. It reads every leasing and resident conversation...and turns them into signals teams can act on now." Site framing: "Your systems report activity, not behavior. They don't show what prospects actually experience. Flair does."

strengths.text: "Call Intelligence: Reads every call, scores agents (human and AI), and surfaces the demand underneath" — coverage of the full call population rather than a sample.
Scores AI leasing assistants as well as human agents, answering a question operators are actively asking: "Is your AI better than your team?"
"Email Shops: Synthetic leads test your follow-up and catch the breaks no one else sees" — an outbound test channel on top of passive call analysis.
"Custom Scorecards: Grade every call & email shop against your criteria, not a generic rubric."
Free introductory secret shops lower the barrier to a first engagement and get them inside accounts without a procurement cycle.
Serves BTR, multifamily, self storage, senior living and student housing; publishes named property management references including CRES and Trion Properties.
Also monitors fair housing compliance and answer rates by property and agent.

gaps.text: Coverage is calls, email, text and interaction tracking; the public product description does not include onsite or video shops of a physical leasing office.
Call intelligence reads conversations the team already handled — by construction it cannot score a prospect inquiry that was never answered, since there is no conversation to read.
The email test channel uses synthetic leads rather than a human shopper's account of the experience.
Public materials describe scoring and signals; they do not describe coaching linked to assigned training courses.

askThis: Are you trying to measure your team's own call handling, or test what an unsolicited prospect actually experiences? Those are two different jobs.
How would you evaluate a community where the phone rang out and nobody called back — what shows up in your data?
What's your plan for the onsite tour and the email follow-up, not just the call?
Once you know an agent is weak on objection handling, what assigns and tracks the training?

objections.objection: Flair reads every call. Why would we pay for a handful of shops?
objections.response: That's a fair question and it's not one I'm going to argue you out of. Reading every call and testing the unsolicited prospect experience are different jobs — call intelligence can only read conversations your team already had. If both matter to you, let me bring in our product team rather than trying to talk you out of the one that fits.

doNotSay: Never claim our shop quality makes conversation intelligence unnecessary — it is a different measurement, and the volume argument is not winnable.
Never assert Flair cannot do onsite or video shops as a capability claim; say their published product description covers calls, email, text and interactions.
Never quote or estimate Flair's pricing.

No employee survey or employee engagement product appears in the published feature set, which is entirely resident-facing.
No commercial real estate tenant survey product.
Company facts are undisclosed: no headquarters, founding year, ownership or pricing on the public site.

whyWeWin: Benchmarked measurement versus feature-level feedback: a score without a peer set does not tell an operator whether they are ahead or behind.
Residents, employees and commercial tenants in one program; Flamingo is resident-only.

The finding routes into assigned training, a policy update and a mystery shop that verifies the change.
askThis: When a Flamingo survey comes back at 4.1, what are you comparing that to?

objections.response: Great — keep it for engagement and service. What it doesn't give you is a peer benchmark, employee listening, or a way to turn a finding into assigned training with verification. Those are different jobs.

objections.objection: Residents already use the app, so response rates are better.
objections.response: That's a real advantage for reach. The gap is on the analysis side: no external comparison set and no employee data to correlate against.

name: Grotto AI
toolCategory: AI conversation intelligence and real-time coaching for multifamily leasing agents

verdict.line: Purpose-built for multifamily, funded by ICONIQ, and coaching agents live on every call and tour — it displaces the reason people buy shops rather than competing with the shops themselves.
verdict.doInstead: This is not a battlecard fight. Do not try to win it by arguing shop quality or shopper training — the buyer is comparing continuous coverage against a sample and you will lose that comparison on its own terms. Qualify what they want to change, then route the deal to product and strategy with the account and the use case. Where the buyer needs an unaffiliated test of the prospect experience — including communities that never answer the phone, email follow-up and onsite behavior — say so plainly and keep the two products in separate lanes.

ownership.value: Private, venture-backed; founders Nick Deveau (CEO) and Ben Epstein (CTO), previously of EvolutionIQ

funding.value: $10M seed announced 19 February 2026, led by ICONIQ, with Asymmetric Capital Partners, Avi Dorfman (Compass co-founder) and Caren Maio (Funnel Leasing co-founder)

pricing.value: No pricing published on the public site.

positioning.value: "AI-powered sales coaching and guidance for multifamily leasing teams" — "Close more leases with Grotto's real-time, AI sales coaching, purpose-built for multifamily," covering the entire prospect lifecycle across calls, tours and written communication.

strengths.text: Purpose-built for multifamily rather than a horizontal sales tool with a multifamily page.
"Call Guidance" delivers "real-time guidance for agents on every call — helping them ask the right questions, handle objections, and book tours" — coaching during the conversation, not after it.
$10M seed led by ICONIQ (February 2026) with multifamily-native angels including Compass and Funnel Leasing co-founders.
Named enterprise customer: Weidner Apartment Homes, which manages over 70,000 units.

Publishes behavioral findings from its own conversation data — agents who laughed with a prospect were "48% more likely to convert a lead to a signed lease," and genuine curiosity correlated with "a 35% increase in conversion." These are Grotto's published claims, not independently verified.
Frames the buy in NOI terms — "recover 8 to 9 figures in NOI and asset value" — which reaches an executive budget that a shop program usually does not.

gaps.text: The product analyzes the operator's own leasing interactions and coaches its own agents; public materials do not describe an independent, unaffiliated third-party shop of the prospect experience.
Because guidance operates during calls and tours the team is already having, there is no described mechanism for evaluating an inquiry that received no response.
Public materials do not describe a human shopper network, video shops, or an industry benchmark dataset.
Traction is described publicly only as "Early customer data points to meaningful improvements in both engagement and conversion" — no published customer count or independently verified results.

askThis: Do you want to coach the conversations you're already having, or find out what happens when a prospect reaches out and nobody responds?
How does Grotto tell you about the community where the phone went unanswered all Saturday?
What covers the email follow-up and the onsite tour experience in your plan?
Once you know which behaviors correlate with conversion, what assigns the training and proves the score moved?

objections.objection: Grotto coaches our agents on every single call. Shops only sample.
objections.response: That's true, and I'm not going to argue the math. They're solving a different problem than an unaffiliated test of the prospect experience. Let me bring in our product team so we're comparing the right things rather than me making a case I can't support.

objections.objection: ICONIQ backed them — they'll win this category.
objections.response: Funding is a signal about the category, not about your portfolio. The useful question is what you're trying to change this year, and whether coverage of your own calls or an outside test of the prospect experience gets you there. Often it's both.

doNotSay: Never argue that human shops make real-time call coaching unnecessary.
Never repeat Grotto's conversion statistics as independently verified fact — they are the vendor's own published claims.
Never state that Grotto has no shopping capability as an absolute; say their public materials describe coaching of the operator's own agents.

name: GROW by Inhabit
toolCategory: Multifamily-native online course library and LMS, sold standalone and bundled with its parent's property management products

verdict.line: A genuine multifamily content competitor with 300+ short courses and named state accreditations, usually discounted into an Inhabit bundle — compete on breadth of compliance coverage, competency evidence and the ability to connect training to operational outcomes.

ownership.value: Owned by Inhabit, a global PropTech company whose brands include ResMan, ResidentIQ, ValenceDocs, Anyone Home, Streamline and others

size.value: Inhabit reports 1,100+ employees worldwide (parent company, not GROW-specific)

pricing.value: Not published. Four purchase models described: a la carte individual courses, bundle with partner Inhabit products (ValenceDocs, APTEXX, Nationwide Compliant, AMS Billing), subscription to the full 300+ course catalog, and one-time SCORM purchase for use in a client's own LMS.

positioning.value: "GROW brings your workplace culture to life by offering short, engaging, relevant courses resulting in productive, valued, happy employees" — training for multifamily and short-term rental property management.

strengths.text: Catalog of over 300 courses spanning 28+ topic areas including leasing, maintenance, operations, fair housing and resident retention.
Named state accreditations: fair housing accredited in Texas and Virginia; human trafficking content meeting Florida and California requirements; Asbestos Class IV aligned to EPA and OSHA standards.
Courses available in SCORM format for one-time purchase and delivery inside a client's existing LMS — a low-commitment entry point that can displace a full platform sale.
Doubles as a company intranet and customizable dashboard, not only a course player.
Custom course development by property management professionals plus upload of a client's existing materials.
Bundleable with Inhabit sibling products, giving the parent a discounting lever in competitive deals.

gaps.text: Published fair housing accreditation covers two states (Texas and Virginia); no broader multi-state approval list is published.
GROW's public site does not describe CEC/credential eligibility (CAM, CAPS, CALP), Spanish or bilingual content, assessments/competency measurement, HRIS integration, or benchmarking.
The customizable-training page describes upload and custom development but does not describe SCORM import, assessment authoring, role-based assignment mechanics or reporting detail.
Branding is fragmented across the parent's estate — the same learning capability is presented as GROW, as ResidentIQ Learning Management and as ResMan Learning depending on the entry point.

whyWeWin: Multi-state portfolios need jurisdiction coverage beyond two states — ask what happens in every state GROW does not publish an accreditation for.
Short courses averaging minutes are good for engagement and weak for proof; ask what evidence exists that someone can do the job, not that they watched the video.
GROW publishes no Spanish/bilingual content claim — if the workforce is bilingual, that is a concrete, checkable difference.
Training that isn't connected to shops, surveys and reputation data can't tell you whether it worked.
askThis: Which states beyond Texas and Virginia are covered for fair housing, and who signs off that the content is current?
How much of the catalog is available in Spanish?
Do the courses carry CEC credit toward CAM, CAPS or CALP?
What does the assessment look like — is there a score, and does it gate anything?
Are you buying the platform or one-time SCORM files? What happens to your completion history in the SCORM model?
If the training bundle is priced against other Inhabit products, what happens to that price if you change any one of them?

objections.objection: GROW has 300+ courses, that's plenty.
objections.response: Course count and coverage aren't the same. Ask how many are fair housing, which states they're accredited in, and how many exist in Spanish — that's where the gap shows up.

objections.objection: We can just buy the SCORM files and run them in our own LMS.
objections.response: That works until the regulation changes. Ask who is responsible for updating a SCORM file you already bought and loaded — and how you'd know it went stale.

objections.objection: It's bundled with our Inhabit products at a good price.
objections.response: Bundle pricing is real leverage on their side. Make sure the comparison is apples-to-apples on jurisdiction coverage and competency evidence before it turns into a price conversation.

doNotSay: GROW has no fair housing content — they publish accreditation in Texas and Virginia.
They have no Spanish content — it is unverified, not disproven.
Any claim about GROW's price, customer count or employee count — none is published.
That GROW and ResMan Learning are definitively the same product — public sources present them as sibling offerings under Inhabit but do not confirm a shared platform.

name: J Turner Research
toolCategory: Multifamily resident feedback and online reputation research

verdict.line: The reputation-score brand of multifamily — strong on reviews and ORA, but they do not publicly disclose the scale or history of their survey benchmark, and there is no training, policy or shop to close the loop.

founded.value: 2003, co-founded by Joseph Batdorf and Nitin Agarwal

ownership.value: Privately held. No acquisition, private equity investment or outside ownership publicly disclosed as of Aug 2026; company pages describe the two founders only.

size.value: 37 team members across 10 states (per company Our Story page)

benchmarkScale.value: 149,000+ properties monitored, 18,346,238 reviews, and 136,225 properties (91%) with at least one review, per the 15th Edition of "The Mechanics of Online Review Sites and ILSs," dated 2026-03-11, which also references a purge of 2M+ historical reviews. The 132,000 figure is still live elsewhere on their own site — quote the dated one.

pricing.value: Entry pricing is published — "as little as $30 per month" across four named tiers (SMART, SMARTER, SMARTEST, GENIUS), described as suggested pairings with custom plans available. No scope is attached to the $30 figure: it is not stated per property, per unit, or per portfolio, and the tier comparison table showed placeholder text at retrieval, so the page appears mid-build. Do not quote $30 as a comparison to our per-unit pricing. If price comes up, the usable line is that they publish an entry point and we can find out what it covers.

positioning.value: "The Only Multifamily Specific, All-In-One Platform Designed to Improve Resident Experience" — surveys, review management, AI-assisted review and survey response, social media management, business listings and ORA monitoring.

strengths.text: The ORA (Online Reputation Assessment) score is an established, widely recognized multifamily standard — a 0-100 score aggregated across 20+ major review sites and ILSs, updated monthly, evaluating feedback across 22 operational areas.
Publishes monthly ORA Power Rankings and year-end summaries that rank properties and management companies, generating durable industry mindshare.
Broad survey line beyond the annual resident survey: resident, prospect, employee, student housing (Spring, Fall, Guarantor, Prospect) and custom surveys in Do-It-Yourself and Made-to-Order formats.
Action Planning Tool (APT) lets teams create and execute S.M.A.R.T. goals against high-priority feedback, and PUSH for Reviews converts survey respondents into public reviewers.
Einstein, their AI tool, is described as having analyzed over 12 million reviews.
Bundles adjacent reputation services — review response, social media management and business listings — into the same platform.
Sells surveys and reputation together to the same multifamily buyer, in one vendor relationship.
ORA is a published, named multifamily reputation metric with a competitor-monitoring product wrapped around it ("intelligence into your high-priority competition").
Response Solutions are marketed as "Review & Survey Response — Powered by AI and Expert Guidance," i.e. a human-supervised managed offering rather than tooling alone.
Business listings management covers "hundreds of business listings for your communities."

gaps.text: Survey benchmark scale and history are not publicly disclosed. Neither the ORA FAQ nor the surveys solution page states the number of survey respondents, the number of participating companies, or the number of years of survey history. The 12-million figure is reviews analyzed by the Einstein AI tool, not survey benchmark scale.
No commercial real estate tenant survey product appears in the published survey line, which covers resident, prospect, employee, student housing and custom surveys.

The published platform is surveys plus reputation; it does not list a training/LMS, policy management or mystery shopping product, so a finding cannot be routed to verified remediation in the same system.
No training, policy or mystery-shopping line is offered — the solutions page lists surveys, reviews, response, social, listings, ORA monitoring and support only.
Review generation / solicitation is not described on the solutions page as a named capability.
Per-tier feature inclusions are not published — the pricing page names four tiers but the comparison table showed placeholder text rather than what each tier includes, as of 2026-08-21.

whyWeWin: Benchmark provenance: the Kingsley Index™ publishes decades of multifamily and commercial real estate benchmarking history; J Turner does not publicly state the scale or history behind its survey comparisons.
CRE tenant surveys: Grace Hill covers commercial tenants alongside residents and employees; J Turner's published survey line does not.

Closed loop: our survey finding assigns training, updates the policy, and a mystery shop verifies the behavior changed — a reputation score tells you the number moved but not why or whether the fix stuck.
A reputation score is an outcome metric. Structured survey data plus benchmarks tells you which operational driver to fix first.

Reputation sits inside PerformanceHQ next to training, policy, surveys and shopping — a recurring review theme can route to a course assignment or a policy acknowledgment without leaving the platform.
Grace Hill can act on the finding, not just report it; a research firm hands you the number and stops.
One vendor for the whole people-and-performance stack reduces the number of integrations and contracts the operator carries.
askThis: When you see your ORA score move, what tells you which operational driver caused it?
How many survey responses and how many companies is your benchmark comparison built from, and over what period?
Do you need to benchmark commercial tenants too? How is that handled today?
Once a survey flags a service or fair housing issue at a property, who assigns the training and how do you verify it took?
Are you paying separately for surveys, review response, social and listings? What does the all-in number look like?
When ORA flags a property, what actually happens on site the next week — who owns the fix?
Are your survey vendor and your review-response vendor the same team, and do their reports reconcile?
Which of your review responses are written by a person and which by a model — and who reviews the fair housing language before it posts?
How is ORA calculated for a property with low review volume, and how do you handle a property that just opened?

objections.objection: ORA is the industry standard — everyone benchmarks on it.
objections.response: ORA is a genuinely well-known reputation score and we don't argue with that. It measures what the public says about you. Our benchmark measures what your residents, employees and commercial tenants tell you directly, against decades of Kingsley data — and then routes the finding into training and a verification shop.

objections.objection: They cover reviews, social and listings in one place.
objections.response: They do, and that's real breadth on the reputation side. The question is what happens after a problem is identified — that's where a training, policy and mystery shop stack changes the outcome rather than the score.

objections.objection: They're multifamily-specific like you are.
objections.response: Agreed. So the comparison narrows to benchmark depth, commercial tenant coverage, and whether a finding can be closed inside the platform.

objections.objection: Our owners already look at ORA.
objections.response: Then keep watching it. The question is what changes the score. Ask them who assigns the training and policy work that moves maintenance and communication themes — that is where PerformanceHQ plugs in.

objections.objection: They're multifamily specialists, you're a platform company.
objections.response: Grace Hill has been multifamily-only for decades across training, policy, surveys and shopping. The specialization argument runs both ways — ours spans the operating problem, not just the measurement.

doNotSay: Do not claim J Turner's data is biased, inflated or compromised. There is no public basis for it and it is a liability statement.
Do not say 'they have no benchmark' — they publish ORA Power Rankings and comparative scoring. Say instead that they do not publicly disclose the scale or history of their survey benchmark.
Do not present the '12 million reviews' figure as survey respondents. It is reviews analyzed by their Einstein AI tool.
Do not quote a J Turner price, client count or revenue figure — none are published.
Do not state that J Turner has been acquired or is PE-owned. No such disclosure was found; if a rep hears otherwise, verify before repeating.
Do not characterize ORA's methodology or claim it is inaccurate — the calculation is theirs and publicly described.
Avoid 'the only platform that connects reputation to training' — a buyer with a browser will find other bundles. State our workflow specifically instead.

Do not raise any claim that RealPage holds exclusive rights to embed ORA scores. The only source is a 2020 press release with no public update, it is under legal review, and it has not been cleared. Awaiting Legal.

methodologyNotes: ORA has been re-baselined twice in ways that moved customer scores. September 2021 added recency weighting, per-site bias normalization and a cross-platform consistency reward — their own communication acknowledged most scores would change, some by 10+ points, and the Elite 1% cutoff would move. Then on 2026-04-22 Apartments.com dropped the CoStar building-quality component, average Apartments.com ratings fell from 4.18 to 3.43 across 65,820 properties, and J Turner reports a +0.15 average ORA change for properties with 10 or more reviews. Describe this as score volatility from upstream model and source changes. Never characterize ORA as inaccurate or inflated.

name: Lattice
toolCategory: Employee performance and engagement platform (HR)

verdict.line: An HR performance platform with an inexpensive engagement add-on — it competes for the employee survey budget; no resident or commercial tenant survey and no multifamily benchmark is described on its public pages.

founded.value: 2015 (Y Combinator company), co-founded by Jack Altman

ownership.value: Private, venture-backed

size.value: Over 485 employees as of January 2022; current headcount unknown

funding.value: $175 million Series F announced January 18, 2022 at a $3 billion valuation, led by Thrive Capital, Elad Gil, Tiger Global and Dragoneer; total funding over $330 million

pricing.value: Published. Engagement $4 per seat per month; Performance $10; Goals & OKRs $8; Foundations bundle $13. Add-ons: Compensation +$6, Grow +$4. Minimum $4,000 annual agreement, billed annually in USD.

positioning.value: A people management platform spanning performance reviews, goals and OKRs, 1:1s, feedback and engagement, with an AI agent and analytics.

strengths.text: Published, transparent per-seat pricing — Engagement at $4 per seat per month makes it easy for an HR buyer to justify.
Engagement module includes pulse surveys, onboarding and exit surveys, eNPS and AI analysis.
Surveys sit inside a broader people-management system — performance reviews, goals, 1:1s, succession planning, calibration — so engagement data lands next to performance data.
Well-capitalized and established: $175M Series F at a $3B valuation, over $330M raised, more than 3,700 businesses as customers as of that announcement.

gaps.text: No resident survey or commercial tenant survey product — the published product line is entirely HR-facing (Performance, Goals & OKRs, Engagement, Compensation, Grow).

No industry benchmark dataset is described for the Engagement module on the pricing page; the only benchmarks referenced are "global benchmarks" within the Compensation add-on, which is compensation data, not engagement.
No multifamily or real estate operator peer comparison is disclosed.
Contract floor of $4,000 per year with annual billing in USD only, which can be a poor fit for smaller operators or non-USD portfolios.
No training/LMS with multifamily compliance content, no policy management and no mystery shopping product.

whyWeWin: Lattice measures employees against Lattice customers in general; Kingsley measures your onsite teams against other property operators.
Residents, employees and commercial tenants in one program — Lattice covers only employees.
Property, region and portfolio rollups instead of org-chart reporting lines.
The finding routes into assigned multifamily training, a policy update and a mystery shop that verifies the change.
askThis: When Lattice reports your engagement score, which peer group is it compared against?
Can you break results out by property and region, or only by manager and department?
Where does resident feedback live, and does anyone correlate the two?
At $4 per seat per month plus the $4,000 minimum, how many seats do you actually need across the portfolio?
After an engagement finding at a property, what training gets assigned and who checks it happened?

objections.objection: HR already runs engagement surveys in Lattice and it's cheap.
objections.response: It is, and for HR-side pulse surveys it does the job. What it does not tell you is how your onsite teams compare to other property operators, and no resident or commercial tenant survey is described on its public pages.

objections.objection: It's only $4 a seat.
objections.response: For the survey mechanism, yes. Price the whole job: the peer benchmark, the resident and commercial tenant side, and the training and verification path. Those aren't in the $4.

doNotSay: Do not quote a Lattice price other than the published figures ($4/seat/month Engagement, $10 Performance, $8 Goals, $13 Foundations, +$6 Compensation, +$4 Grow, $4,000 annual minimum).
Do not state a current Lattice headcount or customer count — the 485-employee and 3,700-customer figures are from January 2022 and are stale.
Do not claim Lattice has no benchmarks at all — the Compensation add-on references global benchmarks. Say that no engagement benchmark scale, and no multifamily peer set, is disclosed.
Do not disparage Lattice's product quality — it is a well-regarded HR platform.

toolCategory: Property operations platform

verdict.line: The one vendor in this set that actually lives in multifamily — but it standardizes tasks, inspections and work orders, not the written policy manual employees acknowledge, so it usually sits alongside us rather than against us.

hq.value: Not published on the vendor's about page

founded.value: 2014, founded by Daniel Cunningham

ownership.value: Private; venture-backed. Not disclosed on the vendor's about page.

size.value: Not published on the vendor site

funding.value: $9.5M investment led by Level Equity, announced September 2020

pricing.value: Not published.

positioning.value: Positions itself as an operating partner for property operations — "we've grown to become one of the most innovative tech companies in multifamily" and "a true operating partner, dedicated to your success," framing the problem as "broken processes and systems" in property operations.

strengths.text: Genuinely multifamily-native: built for multifamily, student housing and other real estate portfolios since 2014 by a multifamily industry veteran.

Broad operational suite — Perform247 (tasks, inspections, code compliance, work orders, document management, unit turns), Acquire247 (due diligence), Protect247 (risk), Connect247 (remote maintenance), Student247.
Strong on the execution side of operations: dynamic custom forms, inspection walks, preventative maintenance schedules, incident reporting and reporting dashboards.
Speaks the buyer's language on risk and code compliance, which makes it credible with the same regional and ops leaders we sell to.

gaps.text: The Perform247 product page centers on custom forms, inspections, work orders, document management and unit turns; it does not describe a prewritten library of multifamily policies, procedures or best practices.
The Perform247 page does not describe policy attestation or acknowledgment tracking, or a compliance calendar for regulatory updates to written policy.
Pricing is not published.

whyWeWin: Different jobs. Leonardo247 standardizes what gets done on site; Grace Hill supplies the written policy that governs how it should be done and the record proving each employee acknowledged it.

Grace Hill ships the content: over a thousand customizable multifamily policies, forms and job descriptions across 18+ manuals covering emergency procedures, leasing, tax credit compliance, maintenance and operations.
Grace Hill maintains the regulatory currency of that content, so fair housing and compliance language does not go stale on the buyer's own writing schedule.
The acknowledgment record — this person, this policy version, this date — is the artifact counsel asks for after an incident, and it sits in PerformanceHQ next to the training that reinforces it.
askThis: Leonardo247 tells your team what tasks to complete. Where does the written policy that governs those tasks live, and who wrote it?
If a fair housing complaint came in, could you produce proof that this employee acknowledged this version of that policy on a specific date?
Does Leonardo247 supply the written policy language, or do you build the forms and instructions yourselves?
When a state or federal rule changes, who rewrites your manual — and how do employees find out?
How does a leasing consultant search for the answer to a policy question mid-conversation with a prospect?

objections.objection: We already have Leonardo247 for operations, so we're covered.
objections.response: Leonardo247 is good at the doing — tasks, inspections, work orders. Ask a different question: where is your written fair housing policy, who wrote it, when was it last updated, and can you prove each employee acknowledged the current version? Those are different problems and most operators run both systems.

objections.objection: They're multifamily and you're multifamily — isn't this the same thing?
objections.response: Same industry, different layer. They standardize execution. We supply the policy library and the compliance record. Plenty of operators use both, and they complement each other cleanly.

Do not disparage Leonardo247's multifamily credibility — it is a legitimate multifamily-native vendor and buyers respect it.
