name: Microsoft SharePoint
toolCategory: General-purpose document management and intranet platform

verdict.line: Not a vendor bake-off — SharePoint is where the buyer's policies already sit, so this is a displacement conversation about content and attestation evidence, never a feature shootout against Microsoft.
verdict.doInstead: Do not attack SharePoint. Let the buyer keep it for files. Ask who writes and updates the policy text today, and who can produce a timestamped acknowledgment record per employee per version at audit — that is the wedge, not document storage.

founded.value: SharePoint first released 2001

ownership.value: Public company (Microsoft Corporation, NASDAQ: MSFT)

size.value: Not published for the SharePoint product specifically

pricing.value: Bundled in most Microsoft 365 business and enterprise plans; standalone SharePoint plans are published by Microsoft. The buyer almost always already pays for it, so incremental cost is effectively zero in their mind.

positioning.value: Microsoft positions SharePoint as "The knowledge platform for Copilot and agents" — content management, AI-powered search, secure sharing and branded intranet hubs.

strengths.text: Already paid for and already deployed at most multifamily operators as part of Microsoft 365 — no new vendor, no new procurement, no new login.

Genuine full-content search: SharePoint indexes the text inside documents, not just titles and metadata, and Microsoft markets AI-powered search that "understands intent and surfaces relevant files and answers."
Mature document versioning, content approval and check-out controls are documented native capabilities.
Unlimited flexibility — permissions, retention, audit policies and Power Automate workflows can be shaped to almost any process.

gaps.text: Microsoft's own document management overview covers versioning, content approval, check-out, retention and audit policies, and does not describe a built-in policy attestation or acknowledgment-tracking feature.

Microsoft's SharePoint product page markets content management, search, sharing and intranet capabilities; it does not offer prewritten policy content of any kind, let alone multifamily policy text — the buyer supplies every word.

Third-party assessment of plain SharePoint for policy management states it "cannot natively ask employees to read and acknowledge a policy, track who has and has not done so, or produce an audit log of attestations," and that there is "no native alert system that tells you a policy is about to expire and needs review" — both require Power Automate configuration or custom development.

whyWeWin: Grace Hill ships the policies. SharePoint ships an empty library. Our Policies library is over a thousand customizable policies, forms and job descriptions written by multifamily experts across 18+ manuals — the buyer starts from written content, not a blank Word document.

Grace Hill maintains regulatory currency as part of the subscription. With SharePoint, somebody on the buyer's payroll owns rewriting the fair housing, leasing and tax-credit language every time a rule changes — and that person usually does not exist.

Attestation evidence is the product, not a workflow the buyer has to build. Grace Hill captures secure electronic acknowledgments tied to a policy version and a person, and assigns automatically by location, position, group or employee.
Policy-to-training linkage lives in PerformanceHQ: the policy the employee acknowledged and the course that teaches it are in the same system, reportable together.

The real cost of SharePoint is not the license. It is the internal author, the Power Automate build, and the person who has to reconstruct an acknowledgment trail out of email the day someone asks for it.
askThis: Who on your team actually writes the policy language today, and when was the emergency-procedures or fair-housing section last rewritten?
If a fair housing complaint came in tomorrow, how long would it take you to produce proof that this specific employee acknowledged this specific version of that policy on a specific date?
When a state rule changes, who finds out, and who edits the document? What is the lag between the rule changing and your manual changing?
Your SharePoint search finds the document. Can it tell a leasing agent the answer to a question at 4pm on a Friday, or does it hand them a 60-page PDF?
How many of your properties are working from a copy of the manual that is no longer the current version?
Did somebody build the acknowledgment workflow in Power Automate? Who maintains it when they leave?

objections.objection: We already have SharePoint and it's free.
objections.response: Agreed — keep it. SharePoint is a good place to store files. What it does not give you is the words. You are still paying somebody to write and re-write every policy, and to rebuild the acknowledgment trail by hand. We ship over a thousand multifamily policies already written and keep them current. Compare our fee to the cost of the person doing that job now.

objections.objection: Our IT team can build acknowledgment tracking in Power Automate.
objections.response: They probably can. The question is whether they should own it for the next five years, and whether the flow they build will hold up as evidence — version-locked, per-person, timestamped — the day it is asked for. That is a maintenance liability you would be taking on to avoid a subscription.

objections.objection: SharePoint search already finds anything.
objections.response: It does — SharePoint content search is genuinely strong, and we're not going to claim otherwise. But search only works on what's written. If the policy text in there is three years old and does not reflect current fair housing guidance, great search just finds the wrong answer faster.

doNotSay: Do not say SharePoint has no search or bad search — it indexes document content and is one of the strongest search engines in this whole comparison set. Claiming otherwise destroys credibility with any IT stakeholder in the room.
Do not say SharePoint 'can't' do attestation. It cannot do it natively, but it can be built. Say 'not native — somebody has to build and maintain it.'
Do not position this as Grace Hill vs. Microsoft. The buyer keeps SharePoint. We are replacing the empty policy folder inside it.
Never disparage the customer's IT team or their existing build.

name: NAVEX One Policy & Procedure Management
toolCategory: GRC / compliance platform

verdict.line: Enterprise GRC with real prewritten policy content — but the content is corporate ethics and compliance (anti-bribery, conflicts of interest, harassment), never fair housing, leasing or tax credit.

founded.value: Not published in the reviewed press materials

ownership.value: Majority stake acquired by a consortium led by Goldman Sachs Alternatives, including Blackstone as a significant minority investor; completed October 14, 2025. Prior majority owner BC Partners retained a significant minority stake.

size.value: NAVEX states it serves 13,000 businesses and organizations globally, including 75% of the Fortune 100 and 500; employee count not disclosed in the release.

pricing.value: Not published.

positioning.value: Frames the problem as policies "buried across different SharePoint sites, shared drives or HR systems" and positions the product as turning "the policy tangle into tidy, time-saving simplicity" inside the NAVEX One GRC platform.

strengths.text: Ships real prewritten content — "ready-to-use, legally-vetted policy templates" covering anti-bribery, conflicts of interest, harassment and other corporate compliance areas. This is one of the few tools in the set that gives the buyer written words, not just a shell.
Full policy lifecycle: version control with complete audit trails, electronic acknowledgment through an employee portal, and legally-sound electronic signature.
Searchable employee portal so staff can find policy content directly, plus multilingual content with parent/child policy workflows for localized variants.
Part of the broader NAVEX One GRC platform, so policy sits alongside hotline, case management and compliance training for enterprise buyers who want one GRC vendor.
Substantial installed base — 13,000 organizations globally including 75% of the Fortune 100 and 500.

gaps.text: The prewritten policy templates NAVEX describes are corporate ethics and compliance topics — anti-bribery, conflicts of interest, harassment. No multifamily, fair housing, leasing or tax credit compliance content is described.
The policy and procedure management page does not describe a standalone vendor-maintained regulatory update service for policy content.
Jurisdiction handling is described as multilingual content with parent/child workflows — a localization and translation model, not published US state-by-state policy variants.
Pricing is not published.

whyWeWin: NAVEX gives an enterprise its code of conduct. Grace Hill gives a multifamily operator its operating manual — over a thousand policies, forms and job descriptions across 18+ manuals covering emergency procedures, leasing, tax credit compliance, maintenance and operations.

Grace Hill's content is maintained against multifamily regulatory change. A corporate ethics library does not track HUD guidance or state landlord-tenant law, so that work would still fall on the buyer's compliance team.
Grace Hill assigns by location, position, group or employee — properties, regions and onsite roles — which is how a multifamily portfolio is actually organized.
Policy links to multifamily training in the same PerformanceHQ platform, written by the same multifamily subject matter experts, so acknowledgment and instruction report together.
askThis: Their template library covers anti-bribery and conflicts of interest. What does it say about fair housing, unit turns, or tax credit file compliance?
Who would write the multifamily-specific manuals, and what is the timeline before your property teams have something to acknowledge?
When HUD guidance or a state rule changes, does NAVEX revise the policy text for you, or notify you that you need to?
Is their jurisdiction capability US state variants of policy text, or translation and localization of one global policy?
How does policy connect to your fair housing training and CEC-eligible courses — same system, same report?
How many multifamily operators can they reference?

objections.objection: NAVEX already gives us prewritten policies, so we don't need your content.
objections.response: They do, and credit where it's due — that's more than most tools here offer. But look at what those policies cover: anti-bribery, conflicts of interest, harassment. Those are corporate ethics policies. Nothing in that library tells a leasing consultant how to handle a reasonable accommodation request or a tax credit file. That is the manual your property teams actually work from, and that's what we write and maintain.

objections.objection: We want one GRC vendor for everything.
objections.response: That's a fair enterprise strategy and we can coexist with it. NAVEX can hold your corporate code of conduct. What it can't do is keep your multifamily operations manuals current, because nobody there is watching fair housing enforcement. Most operators end up needing both layers.

doNotSay: Do not say NAVEX has no prewritten policy content — it explicitly markets ready-to-use, legally-vetted policy templates. The accurate claim is that the content is corporate compliance, not multifamily.
Do not call the product PolicyTech as if it were current branding. NAVEX states PolicyTech has been renamed NAVEX One Policy & Procedure Management. Use both names so the rep is understood.
Do not repeat NAVEX's own ROI figures as if they were independent findings.
Do not quote a price.

verdict.line: OpenSesame is a content aggregator that plugs into whatever LMS the customer already runs — and it is the one vendor in this set that genuinely carries real estate content, through an exclusive IREM collection that includes fair housing, so reps should know it exists rather than be surprised by it.
verdict.doInstead: Do not treat OpenSesame as a rival platform; it has none. Where it appears, ask whether the IREM collection is written for multifamily site operations and multi-state portfolios or for the broader real estate management profession, and whether anyone is mapping it to roles and properties. That gap — curriculum design and assignment, not catalog access — is Grace Hill's ground.

pricing.value: Not published on the vendor site.

positioning.value: A learning platform offering "60,000+ pre-vetted courses in 70+ languages" combined with custom course building and LMS integration — a curated marketplace "matched to your roles, skills, and strategy. Backed by human curators and AI shortcuts."

strengths.text: 60,000+ pre-vetted courses in 70+ languages, positioned for seamless integration into the customer's existing LMS.

gaps.text: OpenSesame is a content marketplace, not a learning platform of record — its own positioning centers on integrating with the LMS the customer already uses.
The IREM collection is described as real estate management covering both residential and commercial; OpenSesame publishes no multifamily-specific, state-by-state compliance curriculum.

whyWeWin: Grace Hill delivers a curriculum mapped to multifamily roles and properties, not a catalog the customer must curate.

positioning.value: AI-powered resident feedback platform that aggregates reviews, surveys, maintenance requests and leasing notes into one dashboard for multifamily, student housing and senior living.

strengths.text: Publishes entry pricing — $99/month tier minimums and a $249 per-property setup fee — which few vendors in this category do.
Property teams control which review sites residents are directed to and at what distribution weight.

The FAQ does not name specific PMS integration partners, deferring to a separate integrations page.

whyWeWin: Grace Hill's survey program is benchmarked against a multifamily dataset, so a score has a comparison set behind it rather than only an internal trend.

Governance matters at portfolio scale — role-based approval on public replies is part of the platform, not an option to switch on.
askThis: If review responses can post fully automatically, who approves the language before it goes live on a fair-housing-sensitive complaint?

At $99 minimums per tier plus $249 per property, what does the real number look like at your unit count?

objections.objection: Opiniion is a fraction of the price.
objections.response: It is priced as a feedback tool, and that is what it is. Compare it against the whole job — benchmarked surveys, response governance, and the training and policy follow-through that changes the score.

objections.objection: We just need more reviews.
objections.response: Volume moves the average for a quarter. Ask what happens to the underlying complaint themes; that is what keeps the average up.

doNotSay: Do not suggest their review solicitation is review gating or non-compliant — there is no public source and the claim carries legal risk.

strengths.text: Deep, purpose-built policy mechanics: version control with archived prior versions, side-by-side change comparison with color-coded highlights, e-signature and acknowledgment tracking, and audit trails.
Full-text keyword search across the policy library, plus a mobile app for staff who are not at desks.
Training assignment linked to policies and job roles, so acknowledgment and instruction connect in one system.
Partner content ecosystem for its own market — accreditation standards manuals and a Lexipol integration for prewritten public safety policy content.
Backed by NEOGOV, which serves nearly 10,000 public sector organizations — real scale and institutional durability behind the product.

gaps.text: PowerDMS markets itself to public safety (law enforcement, 9-1-1, fire, EMS, corrections), healthcare accreditation, government and corporate. Multifamily housing is not among the named markets on its site.

The prewritten policy content available through PowerDMS is public-safety oriented — accreditation standards manuals and a Lexipol integration. No multifamily policy content library is described in its product materials.

whyWeWin: PowerDMS is an excellent system waiting to be filled. Grace Hill arrives with over a thousand multifamily policies, forms and job descriptions across 18+ manuals already written by multifamily experts — the buyer is live on day one, not after a six-month internal writing project.

Our content is maintained for multifamily regulatory change — fair housing, leasing, tax credit compliance, emergency procedures. A public-safety content ecosystem does not cover a single one of those.
Policies and training sit in the same PerformanceHQ platform with the same reporting, and both are multifamily-specific — the policy and the course that teaches it were written by the same people.

askThis: Their policy content partners write for police departments and hospitals. Who would write your fair housing, leasing and tax-credit language?
If you buy PowerDMS, what is your plan for the first 90 days — do you have manuals ready to load, or would somebody be writing them from scratch?

How many multifamily operators are on their reference list, and can you speak to one?
What does implementation include — do they migrate and structure your existing manuals, or is loading content on you?

objections.objection: PowerDMS has better policy workflow features than you do.
objections.response: They have a mature policy engine and we don't dispute that. But every feature they have operates on text somebody still has to write. We give you the text — over a thousand multifamily policies already written and kept current — plus the acknowledgment, version and assignment machinery. Ask yourself which half is harder to build in-house.

objections.objection: They already work with big organizations, so they can handle multifamily.
objections.response: They can technically. The question is content. Their prewritten library and partner ecosystem are built for accreditation and public safety standards. Nothing in it speaks to fair housing, tax credit compliance or unit turns. You would be buying a very good empty container.

doNotSay: Do not claim PowerDMS lacks policy management features — it has version control, redlining, e-signature, acknowledgment tracking and full-text search, all documented publicly.

name: Qualtrics
toolCategory: Horizontal experience management platform

verdict.line: Enterprise-grade survey machinery with a huge cross-industry benchmark, but nothing multifamily-specific — compete on benchmark relevance, time-to-value and the remediation path, never on platform sophistication.

ownership.value: Private. Acquired by Silver Lake and CPP Investments for $12.5 billion; acquisition completed June 2023.

size.value: Unknown — current headcount not verified from a primary source

funding.value: Taken private in a $12.5 billion transaction (2023)

pricing.value: Not published. The Qualtrics pricing page states a pricing philosophy (unlimited users, pay for what you plan to use, flexibility) but lists no plan names with prices or dollar amounts.

positioning.value: An experience management (XM) platform spanning employee experience and customer experience, with Text iQ open-text analysis, lifecycle measurement and action planning; states it serves "more than 8,500 brands."

strengths.text: Very large disclosed EX benchmark: refreshed employee experience benchmarks powered by 32 million respondents from more than a thousand companies globally, on a three-year rolling average covering 2022-2024, with detailed industry cuts.
Text iQ performs open-text analysis at scale, described as eliminating manual analysis to surface insights in free-text employee feedback.
Full employee lifecycle measurement — "measure employee experiences at every major milestone of the employee lifecycle" — plus built-in action planning.
Backed by Silver Lake and CPP Investments after a $12.5 billion take-private, so enterprise buyers face little vendor-viability risk.
Unlimited-user licensing model is part of their stated pricing philosophy, which suits large distributed organizations.

gaps.text: The disclosed EX benchmark is cross-industry with cuts "ranging from information technology to retail"; no multifamily or commercial real estate operator benchmark is disclosed.
No resident survey or CRE tenant survey product is listed in the published product line, which is organized around employee experience and customer experience.
No pricing is published — the pricing page carries no plan names with dollar amounts.
No training/LMS, policy management or mystery shopping product is offered, so a survey finding cannot be routed to verified remediation in the same platform.

whyWeWin: Benchmark relevance beats benchmark size: 32 million cross-industry respondents cannot tell a regional manager how their maintenance response time compares to peer multifamily portfolios. The Kingsley Index™ can.
Out of the box for our industry: our question set, rollups and comparisons are built for property portfolios; Qualtrics is a platform the customer has to configure and staff.
We cover residents, employees and commercial tenants in one place; Qualtrics' published line is employee and customer experience.
Closed loop into training, policy and mystery shop verification — Qualtrics ends at the insight and the action plan.
askThis: Who inside your organization builds and maintains the Qualtrics program — is that a dedicated person, and what does that cost you?
When your engagement score comes back, what are you comparing it against — all industries, or other apartment operators?
Where do resident and commercial tenant feedback live? Same platform, or somewhere else?
How long did it take from signing to your first usable portfolio-level report?
Once a finding lands, who assigns training and who verifies the behavior changed?

objections.objection: Qualtrics is the gold standard and our enterprise already has a license.
objections.response: It's a genuinely excellent platform and we won't argue that. The question is whether your benchmark is relevant. Their published EX benchmark is 32 million respondents across all industries — ours is decades of multifamily and commercial real estate operators. A regional manager needs the second one.

objections.objection: We can build resident surveys in Qualtrics ourselves.
objections.response: You can build the instrument. What you can't build is the peer comparison set, and you'll own question design, distribution, rollup logic and maintenance forever.

objections.objection: It's already paid for by corporate.
objections.response: Then use it where it's strongest and add the industry benchmark and the remediation path where it isn't. Worth asking what the internal admin time actually costs.

doNotSay: Do not suggest Qualtrics is technically weak or lacks features — it is a market-leading enterprise platform and any such claim will be dismissed.

Do not claim Qualtrics 'cannot do' resident surveys. It is a configurable survey platform; the accurate statement is that no resident or CRE tenant product appears in its published line and no multifamily benchmark is disclosed.
Do not quote a Qualtrics price — none is published.
Do not say Qualtrics is financially unstable or being wound down. It is owned by Silver Lake and CPP Investments after a $12.5B take-private.
Do not misstate the 32 million figure as multifamily respondents. It is cross-industry EX benchmark respondents.

name: Radix
toolCategory: Market rent comparables and benchmarking data

verdict.line: Radix runs two data models at once, and the contribution question is no longer the whole conversation. They describe pulling from public sources — scraping rent and availability from property websites, then modeling occupancy, leases and concessions with proprietary algorithms — alongside system-of-record data when a customer contributes it. A prospect can appear in Radix comp sets without contributing anything. The sharper question is which fields are system-of-record and which are modeled, because that is what decides whether a number is observed or inferred.

The about page does not describe the underlying data-collection methodology in detail; the homepage describes a PMS-to-RealRents-to-Analytics flow from participating operators.

Coverage is stated in mixed units across pages — '6 million indexed units' as a 2022 milestone versus '20M+ multifamily units' analyzed on the homepage — with no single current indexed-unit figure published.

whyWeWin: HelloData® does not require the buyer to contribute their own rent roll to a shared pool in order to see comps.
Market data inside a wider Grace Hill platform can be read against onsite execution signals, not only against other rents.

How often does that refresh? Radix publishes a daily comp refresh.

Is there an API, or does the data have to be pulled through the dashboard?

objections.objection: Radix data is better because it comes straight from the PMS.
objections.response: It is a different trade-off: operator-contributed data is precise where operators participate and thinner where they don't, and it usually means contributing your own. Worth checking coverage in your specific submarkets.

doNotSay: Do not claim Radix data is incomplete in a specific market without a source — turn it into a question.

Do not state Radix has no API. They now claim one on a first-party page — "automate document processing via API at scale," alongside named connections to Claude, ChatGPT, Power BI and Databricks. The reference documentation is not public: docs.radix.com is robots-disallowed and help.radix.com is login-gated. The accurate line is "they claim a document-processing API and the reference docs are not public."
Do not quote a Radix price; none is published.

Do not raise Radix's post-termination data rights, and do not characterize their Terms of Service. Their terms do permit perpetual post-termination use of historical customer data, but the wording of any question about it is under legal review and has not been cleared. If a prospect raises vendor data rights unprompted, stay general and escalate.

name: RealPage RealConnect
toolCategory: Learning management system bundled into a property management software platform

verdict.line: Same buyer, same budget line, already inside a stack they own. They publish the category, not the catalog: compliance tracking, learning paths and certification monitoring are all named on their page, but no course titles, counts, jurisdictions, languages or fair housing course are described publicly as of 2026-08-21. RealConnect is also built on the Adobe Learning Manager platform, so platform questions are really Adobe questions. Make the conversation about what is in the library and who maintains it as regulation moves.

ownership.value: Private; acquired by Thoma Bravo, deal completed April 2021

size.value: 7,545 employees (company-wide, not LMS-specific)

pricing.value: Not published.

positioning.value: Describes RealConnect as removing barriers to learning, enhancing the learning experience and establishing learning as a culture to activate employees' potential, with 360-degree content coverage across multifamily soft skills, RealPage product training and custom-created training.

strengths.text: Distributed inside an installed platform base — for existing RealPage clients it is an add-on to an incumbent vendor relationship, not a new procurement.
Mobile-first design explicitly built for just-in-time access on mobile devices.
Learning pathways assignable by position, market type and location.
Fully translated English and Spanish learner interface.
Blended delivery combining self-paced content with live classes.

gaps.text: The product page carries two names — the page is titled RealConnect while RealPage's own customer video collateral still refers to the product as EasyLMS, so buyers encounter inconsistent naming.
The RealConnect product page does not describe fair housing content, state-specific compliance variants, CEC/credential eligibility, SCORM/xAPI import, HRIS integration or benchmarking.
The published language capability is a translated interface (English and Spanish), not a stated count of Spanish-language course content.
No course count or library size is published for the multifamily soft-skills content.

Parent company remains subject to active antitrust litigation and state legislation over algorithmic rent-setting, including a New Jersey Attorney General suit filed April 2025 and RealPage's November 2025 challenge to New York's ban.

whyWeWin: Ask what is actually in the library — RealPage publishes capability language but no course count, no fair housing detail and no state-specific compliance variants on the product page.
A translated interface is not translated content. If half the maintenance team reads Spanish, ask which courses exist in Spanish, not which buttons do.
Compliance defensibility is the buying reason for training. RealPage's page describes dashboards and analytics; it does not describe audit-grade compliance reporting.
Naming inconsistency (RealConnect vs EasyLMS in the same vendor's collateral) is a fair, factual signal to probe on roadmap and investment.
askThis: Is the product you're being quoted called RealConnect or EasyLMS? Which name is on the contract?
How many courses are in the multifamily library, and how many of them are fair housing?
Which courses are available in Spanish — not the interface, the content?
If you're audited on fair housing training, what report do you pull and what does it show?
Which states' compliance variants are included, and who updates them when the law changes?
Can you import your own SCORM courses, and can you export completion history if you leave?

objections.objection: It's included with RealPage, so it's basically free.
objections.response: Bundled and free are different things. Ask what the LMS line adds to the renewal, then ask what's in the library — that's where the value question actually sits.

objections.objection: We're consolidating vendors onto RealPage.

name: RentCast
toolCategory: Self-serve rent estimate, property record and market data API

verdict.line: RentCast sells $12-a-month rent estimates to individual investors and landlords and a $74-$449/month property-data API to developers — it is not bidding against HelloData® for institutional multifamily revenue-management budget, so treat it as an adjacent consumer/SFR tool, not a rival.
verdict.doInstead: If a prospect raises RentCast, do not run a feature comparison. Ask what decision they are trying to make: if it is underwriting a single rental or checking one address, RentCast is a reasonable free tool and saying so builds credibility. If it is pricing a portfolio of communities against live competitor concessions, point out RentCast's market data is zip-code level and its comps are per-property, then move the conversation to portfolio-level comps, concessions and the operational signal around them.

founded.value: 2020, by Anton Ivanov, who also founded the real estate analysis platform DealCheck. RentCast's about page states it was built by 'experienced real estate investors and engineers' who previously worked on DealCheck.

ownership.value: Private, for-profit. Crunchbase lists the legal name as Fortnoff Financial LLC.

size.value: 1-10 employees per Crunchbase. No headcount figure is published on RentCast's own site.

funding.value: No funding rounds are listed on the Crunchbase profile, and no funding or investor information appears on RentCast's own about page. Whether the company is self-funded is not publicly stated.

pricing.value: Published, unusually for this category. Web app: Free plan $0 (5 nearby rental comps, 5 properties tracked); Pro $12/month billed annually or $19/month billed monthly (20 nearby comps, 50 properties), with 'Contact us for custom pricing' above 50 units. API: Developer $0/month for 50 requests ($0.20 per request overage); Foundation $74/month for 1,000 requests ($0.06 overage); Growth $199/month for 5,000 requests ($0.03 overage); Scale $449/month for 25,000 requests ($0.015 overage); custom enterprise plans on request. API billing is monthly with no long-term contracts.

positioning.value: Self-serve rental data for the individual investor: 'Look up accurate rent prices and comps for any property, and track your rental portfolio with real-time alerts and market updates.' Describes itself as 'An Essential Platform for Real Estate Investors and Property Managers', for those 'just starting out or manag[ing] hundreds of units'. The stated mission is 'building the best platform for accessing real-time property and rental data in the United States', on the belief that 'everyone should have access to accurate, real-time property and rental data'.

strengths.text: Large published record count: '150+ million residential and commercial properties' in the database, with nationwide US coverage and market data for '38,000+ zip codes'.

Daily collection cadence: 'We scan and catalog new and updated rental listings daily', with 'over 500 thousand record and listing updates daily' and updated data 'immediately available via our API without delays or caching'.
A real, documented, self-serve REST API with public pricing and a free tier — a developer can be pulling property records the same day without a sales conversation.

Breadth of data types beyond rent: property records, structural attributes, tax assessment history, owner details, sale transaction history, value and rent estimates, comps, and active for-sale and for-rent listings across all 50 states.
Published, aggressively low pricing removes a procurement barrier: a Free plan at $0 and Pro at $12/month billed annually.

Transparent estimate methodology for the buyer — rent estimates are 'calculated in real time based on the available rental data' using 'a proprietary weighted average formula', and users can view the specific comparable properties used plus an estimate range, not just a point estimate.

gaps.text: Market statistics are zip-code level only — the market statistics endpoint 'accepts a valid 5-digit US zip code' as its required parameter. No submarket construct is described on the pages reviewed.
Concession, specials or lease-up incentive data is not described on the pricing page, the API product page, the market statistics endpoint reference, or the rental data sources help article.

Rental market history begins April 2020 and sale market history begins January 2024, and the documentation warns 'There may be gaps in the historical data when there were not enough listings to generate statistically significant averages'.

Coverage is qualified in RentCast's own words as 'nationwide coverage for most residential and commercial properties in the US, as well as sale and rental market data coverage for most US zip codes and cities' — 'most', not all.

The web app's published plans cap portfolio tracking at 5 properties (Free) and 50 properties (Pro), with anything larger routed to 'Contact us for custom pricing' — the productised offering is scoped to small portfolios.

No enterprise tier, institutional pricing or dedicated large-account support is described in the API help article; the stated audience is developers wanting to 'power your real estate applications, CRMs and workflows'.

Data is compiled by scanning 'rental property listings from various public sources, including online records, directories, and public domain information' plus 'public county records, recorded deeds, tax assessor databases, and online directories' — there is no operator-contributed or property-website channel described, so unit-level pricing at a specific apartment community depends on that community appearing in scanned listing sources.
Crunchbase lists the company at 1-10 employees with no funding rounds — a materially different scale of engineering and support capacity than the venture-backed multifamily data vendors.

whyWeWin: Different buyer, different job. RentCast answers 'what should I charge for this house?' for one owner. HelloData® answers 'how is my portfolio priced against live competitor rents and concessions this week?' for an operator running communities.
Concessions are the number that moves effective rent in multifamily, and they are the number RentCast does not describe collecting.
Zip codes are not submarkets. An institutional pricing decision needs a comp set the operator defines, not a postal boundary.
HelloData® sits inside a Grace Hill platform where the market signal can be read against training, shop, survey and reputation data — the rent moved, but was it the market or was it your team?
askThis: Are you using RentCast to underwrite individual acquisitions, or to price your communities week to week? Those are different problems.
When a comp two blocks away drops six weeks free, where do you see it today?
Is a zip code a useful comp boundary in your markets, or do you define your own comp set?
How far back does your history go for the submarkets you actually price against?
Who on your team owns pricing, and what do they open on Monday morning?

objections.objection: We already use RentCast and it costs us almost nothing.
objections.response: It is a genuinely good tool for what it does, and at $12 a month there is no reason to drop it. It is answering a property-level question, though. If the decision you are making is portfolio pricing against live competitor concessions, that is a different dataset — worth looking at what you would need on top.

objections.objection: Their API is $449 a month for 25,000 requests. Why would we pay more?
objections.response: You are comparing a per-request data feed to a pricing product. The API charge is for records; the question is who assembles those records into a comp set, tracks concessions, and puts it in front of the person setting rents. If your team wants to build that themselves, RentCast is a reasonable input.

objections.objection: 150 million properties is more coverage than HelloData®'s 5 million.
objections.response: Those numbers count different things. RentCast counts every residential and commercial property record in the US, mostly single-family. HelloData®'s number is multifamily properties with live rent and concession data. Depth on the assets you compete with matters more than a national record count.

doNotSay: Do not say RentCast has no concession data. Say concession tracking is not described on their pricing page, API documentation or help articles.
Do not call RentCast a toy or imply the data is inaccurate — they document their sources and their estimate methodology publicly, and a prospect who uses it will hear the dismissal as uninformed.
Do not claim RentCast cannot serve large portfolios. Their pricing page routes 50+ units to custom pricing, and they reference custom enterprise API plans.
Do not compare the 150M property figure to HelloData®'s 5M as if it were the same measure — it is not, and the comparison is unfavourable and misleading at the same time.
Do not present RentCast as a competitor in a deal review. Nothing in the public evidence shows them bidding for institutional multifamily pricing budget.

verdict.doInstead: Treat Rentgrata as a leasing and referral tool that coexists with Grace Hill Surveys — never as a survey alternative. If it comes up, use it as a discovery hook: ask what the operator uses for structured, benchmarked resident and employee listening, and separately qualify whether the Opiniion platform (review and feedback collection) is in the account following the August 2025 acquisition. Compete against Opiniion, not Rentgrata.

ownership.value: Acquired by Opiniion, announced August 4, 2025

positioning.value: An AI-powered platform connecting apartment prospects with current residents ("Resident Ambassadors") for private conversations about the community, with rewards paid to both parties on move-in, and "Ari by Rentgrata" generating aggregated anonymized insights from those conversations.

strengths.text: Well-defined niche with disclosed traction: 350,000+ renter conversations, 65,000 move-ins and 1,500+ communities served.

Ari by Rentgrata generates aggregated, anonymized insights from prospect-resident conversations to identify community trends and improvement areas — an unstructured feedback signal adjacent to surveys.
Double-sided reward model (prospect and resident both receive a bonus on move-in) creates a direct leasing conversion mechanic, not just a feedback channel.
Acquisition by Opiniion in August 2025 pairs the conversation platform with review management capability, broadening the combined offering.

gaps.text: Not a survey product. The published product line is resident ambassador conversations, rewards, lead conversion and AI insights; surveys, benchmarking and review platforms are not described as core features.
No industry benchmark dataset is described, so nothing produces a comparable score against peer operators.
No employee survey or commercial tenant survey capability appears in the published product line.
Ari's insights are drawn from self-selected prospect-resident conversations, not a structured sampling instrument, so they are directional rather than measurable.
No pricing is published.

whyWeWin: Not applicable as a head-to-head — Rentgrata and Grace Hill Surveys solve different problems and can coexist in the same account.

If the buyer treats Ari's conversational insights as their listening program, the distinction to draw is structured, benchmarked measurement versus directional signal from self-selected conversations.

pricing.value: Not published. A pricing page is linked but shows no tiers or costs.

positioning.value: Self-described as "The #1 AI-Powered Reputation Management Software," turning reviews, listings and surveys into actionable intelligence for multi-location brands.

strengths.text: Multifamily / property management is a named industry vertical with a dedicated real-estate solution page.
Lifecycle review requests (renewal, post-maintenance) triggered from PMS integrations with Yardi, Entrata and RealPage.
Competitive Insights tracks nearby-community ratings, themes and response times; Portfolio Benchmarking flags outlier properties.
Corporate → regional → property permission model with pre-approved templates and approval workflows for fair-housing-sensitive language.
Reputation IQ supports plain-language questions across resident data; Rep Score rolls signals into one KPI.

whyWeWin: Grace Hill's reputation data lives beside training completion, policy attestation, survey scores and shop results, so a regional can see whether the fix actually happened.
Fair housing is not a template setting for us — it is the same content library the onsite team is trained and tested on.

objections.response: So do we, and integration is table stakes now. The differentiator is whether the reputation signal reaches the person who can fix it.

toolCategory: Learning module bundled into a property management system, combining PMS product training with a multifamily course library

verdict.line: Usually not chosen — it's already in the ResMan contract, so you're displacing an included module: make the buyer articulate what the 300 short courses actually prove, and where jurisdiction coverage and competency evidence run out.

ownership.value: ResMan is an Inhabit brand; Mainsail Partners announced ResMan's transition into the Inhabit IQ portfolio

size.value: Inhabit reports 1,100+ employees worldwide (parent company, not product-specific)

pricing.value: Not published.

positioning.value: Positioned around team performance and culture — delivering information and tools so teams reach their full potential, with ResMan University included for training on the ResMan platform itself.

strengths.text: More than 300 courses covering fair housing, harassment, customer service, leasing, risk management and safety.
ResMan University is included, covering training on the ResMan platform itself — one system for both product enablement and industry training.
Short-format courses averaging about eight minutes, designed for retention and completion.
Explicitly serves affordable housing employees alongside conventional multifamily; ResidentIQ variant adds student housing role content.
Doubles as a custom company intranet for employee communications.
Custom content creation and upload, plus customizable dashboard branding.

gaps.text: The ResMan Learning page does not describe state-specific compliance courses, CEC/credential eligibility, role-based assignment, assessment types or scoring, SCORM support, mobile functionality, Spanish/bilingual content, HRIS integration or pricing.
Fair housing is listed as a topic but no state accreditation or approval is published for the ResMan-branded offering.

The same underlying capability is marketed under at least three names (ResMan Learning, ResidentIQ Learning Management, GROW), which makes it hard for a buyer to establish which product and roadmap they are actually buying.
No benchmarking against industry data is described.

whyWeWin: An included module gets used because it's there, not because it's proven — make the buyer state what evidence of competency they can currently produce.
Fair housing appears as a topic without a published state approval; multi-state and affordable portfolios need jurisdiction coverage they can defend in an audit.
Eight-minute courses drive completion, not capability. Position Grace Hill on competency assessment and role depth.
Training that isn't wired to survey, shop and reputation data can't show whether the property changed.

If you're audited tomorrow on fair housing training for a specific property, what report do you produce?
Are courses assigned by role and property automatically, or does someone assign them manually?
Is there a passing score, and what happens when someone fails?
Is any of the content available in Spanish?
Is the learning module a separate line on your ResMan invoice, or bundled? What is it actually worth to you?

objections.objection: It's already included with ResMan.
objections.response: Included is a cost argument, not an outcome argument. Ask what it currently proves in an audit and whether anyone has checked the fair housing coverage against your states.

objections.objection: 300 courses is more than we'd ever use.
objections.response: Usually true — which is why the number isn't the point. The question is whether the ten courses that carry real legal exposure are current, jurisdiction-correct and assessed.

objections.objection: We like that ResMan University and industry training are in one place.
objections.response: That's genuinely convenient. Worth separating the two jobs though: product enablement and compliance defensibility have very different standards of proof.

doNotSay: They have no fair housing training — fair housing is explicitly listed in their catalog.
They're just a reskinned GROW — public sources do not confirm a shared platform.

verdict.line: Rilla records and analyzes the operator's own onsite tours and explicitly markets itself as faster than in-person mystery shopping — a horizontal category leader now selling directly into the multifamily tour budget.
verdict.doInstead: Do not treat this as a battlecard fight and do not argue shop quality — their pitch is coverage and speed of feedback, and that comparison is not winnable on its terms. verdict.line: Deep multifamily survey line paired with the ApartmentRatings review site under Internet Brands — compete on benchmark disclosure, commercial tenant coverage and the ability to close the loop into training and mystery shopping.

hq.value: Unknown — not disclosed on the SatisFacts site; parent Internet Brands is headquartered in El Segundo, CA

founded.value: SatisFacts Research founded by Doug Miller (per Swift Bunny launch release, which describes him as "the founder of SatisFacts Research"); exact founding year not disclosed on the SatisFacts site

ownership.value: Owned by MH Sub I, LLC dba Internet Brands. Internet Brands (owner of ApartmentRatings.com) acquired SatisFacts Research in July 2012 and combined the two.

size.value: Unknown — headcount not disclosed

pricing.value: Not published. No rates disclosed on the products or homepage.

positioning.value: "The leading provider of resident surveys focusing on multifamily retention and reputation management" — an integrated survey plus reputation stack sold under the joint SatisFacts & ApartmentRatings brand, anchored by the epIQ Index.

strengths.text: Broad multifamily survey line: Annual resident satisfaction survey, Insite event-triggered feedback surveys, FLEX customizable surveys, Takeover surveys for pre-acquisition assessment, and an Employee Feedback Survey.

The epIQ Index (Experience & Performance Intelligence Quotient) is positioned as a single letter-grade performance metric combining verified ApartmentRatings and SatisFacts data across four variables on a rolling 365-day period, updated daily.
Owns distribution: ApartmentRatings.com profiles more than 150,000 communities across the U.S., giving SatisFacts a review-site footprint most survey vendors do not have.
Explicitly ties employee engagement to resident outcomes, positioning the employee survey to show "how your employees' level of engagement directly impacts resident loyalty and revenue growth."

Full reputation stack alongside surveys: Verified Review Program, Review Responder (claimed "5.5x faster" responses), Reputation Management across 100+ sites, Google Direct, and the LEO all-in-one bundle.

Runs a national awards program with published, specific eligibility thresholds — 2024 winners required a minimum of 100 (management company) or 25 (community) Insite or Annual survey completions and a portfolio score of 4.25 or above out of 5.0; 3,445 communities nationwide qualified.
Review Responder is a managed service: responses are "crafted by industry experts — all within 24 business hours."
Broad multifamily survey line — Annual Resident Satisfaction, Insite touchpoint, Employee, FLEX and Takeover (due-diligence) surveys.
Structural tie to ApartmentRatings and the epIQ Index report card, a review property multifamily owners already track.
Verified Review Program and Google Direct give solicited reviews a route onto sites that matter to leasing.

gaps.text: Survey benchmark scale and history are not disclosed. Neither the homepage, products page nor the epIQ Index page states total survey respondents, number of participating companies, or years of survey history; the only history claim found is "over 10 years of historical data" attached to their biennial Online Renter Study, not the survey benchmark.
No commercial real estate tenant survey product appears in the published product line, which is multifamily resident and employee only.

The epIQ Index is composed of review ratings, review count per unit, manager review engagement rate and manager reply time — three of the four inputs measure review-response behavior rather than operational service quality.
The published product line covers surveys and reputation; it does not list a training/LMS, policy management or mystery shopping product.
No pricing is published.
No training, policy management or mystery-shopping line — the product suite is surveys plus reputation only.
No pricing is published anywhere on the site.
Competitor benchmarking is not described as a product capability on the site's solution pages.

whyWeWin: Benchmark disclosure and depth: the Kingsley Index™ publishes decades of multifamily and CRE benchmarking history; SatisFacts does not publicly disclose the scale or history behind its survey comparisons.
CRE tenant surveys: Grace Hill covers commercial tenants; the SatisFacts line does not.
Closed loop: a survey finding routes into assigned training, a policy update and a mystery shop that verifies the change — SatisFacts stops at survey and review response.
Independence: our benchmark and our reporting are not tied to a consumer review property, so there is no question about how the two interact.
PerformanceHQ turns a review theme into an assignment — training, policy acknowledgment or a shop — inside the same platform the survey data lives in.
Grace Hill's survey benchmark and reputation view sit in the same reporting layer as workforce data, so a regional manager sees cause and effect on one screen.
Our reputation offering is not tied to a review site we also operate, which removes a conflict-of-interest question some owners raise.
askThis: Your survey vendor and the public review site are the same company. How do you think about that when you're reading your own score?
How many survey responses and how many companies sit behind the benchmark you're compared to, and over how many years?
Three of the four epIQ inputs relate to reviews and how fast managers reply. How do you separate 'we respond quickly' from 'the service is actually good'?
Do you need commercial tenant surveys as well? Where does that live today?
When a survey flags an issue at a property, who assigns the training, and how do you verify the behavior changed?
Who owns your epIQ score internally, and what do they do with it in a given month?
When your survey vendor and your review vendor are the same company, how do you separate what residents told you privately from what they posted publicly?
How long does a response actually take to appear on Google after a one-star review lands on a Friday?
What happens to a recurring maintenance complaint after it shows up in both the survey and the reviews?

objections.objection: SatisFacts has been doing multifamily resident surveys longer than almost anyone.
objections.response: True, and their survey line is genuinely deep. The comparison is on benchmark transparency, whether commercial tenants are in scope, and what happens after the finding lands.

objections.objection: We get surveys and our ApartmentRatings presence from one vendor.
objections.response: That's a real convenience. It's also worth asking how you'd read your own numbers if the benchmark and the public review site sat with two independent parties.

objections.objection: epIQ gives us one score to manage to.
objections.response: It's a clean number. Just note what it's made of — review ratings, review volume per unit, manager response rate and reply time. Faster replies move it. Fixing the underlying service issue is a different exercise, and that's where training, policy and a verification shop come in.

objections.objection: They already own ApartmentRatings, so their data is better.
objections.response: It is one source among many. Ask what share of your prospect traffic comes from ApartmentRatings versus Google, and whether your reputation strategy should be organized around a single site's index.

objections.objection: We already use SatisFacts for surveys, adding response is easy.
objections.response: It is easy — and it stops at the reply. Ask what happens after the reply: who is assigned what, and where is the proof the number moved.

doNotSay: Never assert that SatisFacts or ApartmentRatings data is biased, manipulated or compromised because the survey vendor and review site share an owner. There is no public evidence for it, it is defamatory in tone, and it is a legal risk. Ask the neutral question instead — it is in askThis.
Do not say 'they have no benchmark' — the epIQ Index and their national awards program are public. Say that the survey benchmark's scale and history are not publicly disclosed.
Do not claim the 150,000+ figure is survey respondents. It is the number of communities profiled on ApartmentRatings.com.
Do not attribute Internet Brands corporate facts (revenue, headcount, other properties) to SatisFacts.
Do not quote a SatisFacts price or client count — none are published.
Do not say SatisFacts does not do employee surveys — an Employee Feedback Survey is in their published line.
Do not claim SatisFacts manipulates ApartmentRatings ratings — there is no public source for that and it is legally risky.
Do not say they 'have no benchmarking' — say it is not described on their public product pages.

name: Status Quo — DIY surveys or no formal listening program
toolCategory: In-house survey effort using a free tool, a spreadsheet, or no formal listening program at all

verdict.line: The most common competitor in the set and the hardest to dislodge — never mock it, credit what it genuinely gets right, then compete on the one thing it structurally cannot produce: a comparison to peer operators.

pricing.value: Effectively free in hard dollars — a free survey tool, an existing spreadsheet, or nothing at all. The real cost is staff time, which is rarely tracked.

positioning.value: "We already know what our residents think — our managers talk to them every day, we read every review, and we send a survey once a year."

strengths.text: It costs nothing in hard dollars and requires no procurement, no security review and no new contract — a real advantage when budgets are tight.
The questions are exactly the questions leadership wants answered, with no vendor's standard instrument in the way.
Nobody has to learn a new system, and there is no implementation project competing for onsite attention.

Experienced operators genuinely do know a great deal about their properties. A good regional manager walking a site picks up things no survey captures, and dismissing that instinct is the fastest way to lose the room.
Reading reviews is free, immediate and unfiltered — it is real feedback, and operators who do it consistently do catch problems.
Zero vendor risk: no renewal, no price increase, no dependency on someone else's roadmap.

gaps.text: No external comparison. A score of 78 with no peer set cannot tell an operator whether they are winning or losing — this is a structural property of any in-house instrument, not a claim about a specific vendor.

Reviews are a self-selected sample. Residents who post are disproportionately those with a strong grievance or a strong attachment; the quiet majority whose renewal decision is actually in play is largely absent.
An annual survey surfaces a problem up to twelve months after it started, by which point the affected residents have already made renewal decisions.
Question wording usually drifts year over year in a DIY instrument, which quietly destroys the ability to trend results reliably.
Response rates are typically not managed — no reminder cadence, no channel testing, no non-response analysis — so results skew toward whoever happened to open the email.
Employee feedback is usually absent entirely, so an operator cannot see the link between team engagement and resident outcomes.
Commercial tenants, where a portfolio has them, are almost never surveyed under a DIY program.
Results live in a spreadsheet with no property, region or portfolio rollup, so the executive view has to be rebuilt by hand each cycle.
Nothing connects a finding to remediation: no assigned training, no policy update, no verification that the behavior changed.
The program depends on one person. When that analyst or marketing coordinator leaves, the survey usually stops.
The staff time cost is real but invisible, because it is never priced against the free tool it replaces.

whyWeWin: The Kingsley Index™ answers the one question no in-house survey can: is a 78 good for a portfolio like yours?
Decades of multifamily and commercial real estate benchmarking history means the comparison holds up in an investor conversation, not just an internal one.
Residents, employees and commercial tenants in one benchmarked program instead of three disconnected efforts.
A consistent instrument means year-over-year trending actually works.
Continuous, event-triggered listening finds the problem in the week it happens instead of at the next annual cycle.
The finding routes into assigned training, a policy update, and a mystery shop that verifies the behavior changed — the DIY path ends at the chart.
askThis: When your survey comes back at 78, how do you know whether that's good?
How would you explain that number to an investor or a lender who asked how you compare to peer operators?
Who owns running the survey today, and what happens to the program if that person leaves?
Did the questions change between last year's survey and this year's? Can you still trend it?
What was your response rate, and do you know how the people who didn't answer differ from the people who did?
Are you measuring your onsite teams as well as your residents? Can you tell whether turnover at a property is driving the resident scores?
When last year's survey flagged a maintenance issue at three properties, what happened next — and how did you confirm it got fixed?
Roughly how many hours did the last survey cycle take across your team, start to finish?

objections.objection: We already do our own survey and it works fine.
objections.response: That's genuinely more than a lot of operators do, and it means you already believe in listening. The one thing it can't give you is context — a 78 with no peer set doesn't tell you whether to celebrate or act. That's what the benchmark adds.

objections.objection: Our managers already know what residents think.
objections.response: Many of them do, and the good ones are usually right. The problem is you can't roll up instinct across 40 properties, defend it to an investor, or trend it year over year. The survey doesn't replace their judgment — it makes it comparable.

objections.objection: We read every review, that's our feedback loop.
objections.response: Reviews are real feedback and worth reading. They're also self-selected — you hear from the delighted and the furious. The residents whose renewal is genuinely undecided rarely post, and those are the ones the number depends on.

objections.objection: We don't have budget for this.
objections.response: Fair. Worth pricing the current approach honestly, though — the hours to build, send, chase, clean and roll up the survey, plus the cost of finding out about a problem eleven months late.

objections.objection: We'd rather build it ourselves in a tool we already have.
objections.response: You can build the instrument. What you can't build is the peer comparison set, and you'll own question design, response-rate management and rollup logic permanently.

doNotSay: Never mock or belittle the buyer's current approach. They built it, they may have defended it internally, and insulting it makes the decision personal.
Do not claim the buyer 'has no idea' what residents think. Many experienced operators have accurate instincts, and telling them otherwise ends the conversation.
Do not invent a statistic about what DIY surveys cost, what response rates they achieve, or how much revenue poor listening loses. If you need a number, ask the buyer for theirs.
Do not cite an industry study, retention percentage or ROI figure unless it is a Grace Hill-approved, sourced claim.
Do not claim reviews are worthless — they are useful and free, just self-selected.
Do not promise a specific score improvement, retention lift or NOI impact from switching.

sv-resident.note: A free tool can send a resident survey; what it cannot do is benchmark, trend reliably or manage response rates.

sv-employee.note: Varies by operator. In practice, employee listening is usually absent or handled ad hoc by HR.

sv-cre-tenant.note: Commercial tenant surveys are almost never run under a DIY program.

sv-benchmark-dataset.note: There is no external comparison set. This is the defining structural limitation of the status quo.

sv-benchmark-scale.note: No benchmark exists, so no scale or history can be disclosed. The buyer's own historical data is the only comparison available, and only if question wording stayed consistent.

sv-portfolio-rollup.note: Rollups are rebuilt by hand in a spreadsheet each cycle, if at all.

sv-lifecycle.note: Typically a single annual send; event-triggered lifecycle surveys require automation the status quo does not have.

sv-custom-questions.note: Full control over questions is the status quo's genuine strength — though without a benchmarked core, the answers have nothing to be compared against.

sv-sentiment.note: Open-text responses are read manually, if at all.

sv-investor-grade.note: An unbenchmarked internal score does not stand up in an investor or lender conversation.

sv-action-planning.note: No structured action planning; follow-up depends on whoever reads the spreadsheet.

sv-published-pricing.note: Free or near-free in hard dollars — the staff time cost is real but untracked.

verdict.line: The most common competitor in the pipeline is a regional manager with a spreadsheet — respect that it works and costs nothing on paper, then compete on independence, consistency and whether anyone can prove the coaching changed the score.

pricing.value: No line-item cost. The spend is regional manager and marketing coordinator time, which sits inside payroll rather than a vendor budget.

positioning.value: "We already do this ourselves." A regional walks the property, calls a few communities as a prospect, phones competitors for rents and specials, and puts the results in a shared spreadsheet reviewed at the monthly ops meeting.

strengths.text: It is genuinely free at the point of use — no procurement, no contract, no vendor onboarding, no budget line to defend.
The person doing the evaluation already knows the property, the team, the submarket and the history, so context that a third-party shopper misses is built in.
Feedback is immediate and personal. A regional who hears a bad call can coach that afternoon rather than waiting for a report.
Comp shops phoned in by the team produce current rent and concession intelligence that also feeds pricing decisions — one activity, two uses.
Nothing is hidden behind a vendor's methodology. The operator controls exactly what gets asked and can change it the same day.
For a small portfolio with a hands-on regional, this is often sufficient — and telling that buyer otherwise is how you lose credibility.

whyWeWin: A shopper the team does not recognize gets the experience a real prospect gets; a regional the team recognizes gets the experience the team performs.
One rubric applied across every community means a 78 in one region is comparable to a 78 in another, which a spreadsheet of different people's impressions cannot deliver.
The evaluation is documented and time-stamped by a third party, which matters when a fair housing question arrives.
The score assigns the training and the retest proves it moved — the loop closes without anyone remembering to close it.
Regional manager hours spent shopping are hours not spent on occupancy, and that cost is real even though it never appears on an invoice.
askThis: How many of your communities got shopped last quarter — not planned, actually shopped?
Does the team know when a regional is shopping them? What happens to the result when they do?
If two regionals score the same call, do you get the same number?
When a shop surfaces a fair housing risk, what's the documented record six months later if someone asks?
What does a regional's day cost you, and how many of those days go into shopping and comp calls each month?
Show me the last time a low score turned into training that someone completed — where would I see that?

objections.objection: We already do this ourselves and it works fine.
objections.response: For a lot of operators it does, and I'm not going to tell you it doesn't. The two things it can't give you are independence — your team knows the regional's voice — and consistency, so scores compare across regions and over time. If neither of those is a problem for you today, keep doing what you're doing.

objections.objection: It's free.
objections.response: It's off-budget, which isn't the same thing. Count the regional hours and the comp-call hours per month. Then ask what those hours would have earned somewhere else. The question isn't whether to spend, it's what you're already spending and what you get back for it.

objections.objection: Our regionals know the properties better than any outside shopper would.
objections.response: True, and that's an advantage for coaching. It's a disadvantage for measurement — the team performs differently for someone they recognize. Use both: their judgment for coaching, an outside read for the baseline.

doNotSay: Never tell a buyer their internal process is amateur or unserious — it is usually run by the most committed operator in the building.
Never quote a savings or ROI figure for replacing internal shops; we have no sourced number for their internal cost.
Never imply their team is dishonest. The issue is that people behave differently for someone they recognize, not that anyone is cheating.

name: SurveyMonkey
toolCategory: General-purpose online survey tool

verdict.line: The cheap, familiar way to send a survey — it gives you a distribution mechanism and a generic benchmark, not a multifamily peer comparison or anyone accountable for what the answer means.

founded.value: 1999, by Ryan Finley (later joined by Chris Finley)

ownership.value: Private. Rebranded to Momentive Global in June 2021; a Zendesk acquisition was rejected by shareholders in 2021; acquired by a Symphony Technology Group-led consortium for $1.5 billion, completed May 2023, after which the company reverted to the SurveyMonkey brand.

size.value: Unknown — current headcount not verified. Scale reported as over 250,000 organizations and 42 million users globally.

funding.value: Acquired for $1.5 billion by an STG-led consortium (2023)

pricing.value: Published. Team Advantage $30 per user per month and Team Premier $92 per user per month, both billed annually with a 3-user minimum; Enterprise is custom-quoted with a 5-user minimum.

positioning.value: A SaaS provider of online survey and forms tools, with question banks, expert-certified templates and optional industry benchmarks.

strengths.text: Published, self-serve pricing — a buyer can price it without a sales call: Team Advantage $30/user/month, Team Premier $92/user/month, billed annually.
Enormous familiarity and reach: over 250,000 organizations and 42 million users, supported in 56+ languages across 190+ countries.
Offers both free Global Benchmarks (with Question Bank questions) and paid Industry Benchmarks, with some paid plans including one industry benchmark free.
Extremely low barrier to entry and near-zero training requirement, which is why it wins the 'we'll just do it ourselves' decision.

gaps.text: Benchmark scale is minimally disclosed — the benchmarks page states only that a benchmark requires responses from "30+ organizations," with no total response count, company count by industry or number of industries covered.
Benchmark data is limited to select Question Bank questions and is available in English only.
No multifamily or commercial real estate benchmark is offered; benchmarks are generic industry cuts on standardized questions.
No resident, CRE tenant or property-portfolio survey product exists — the product is a general-purpose survey builder, so question design, rollup logic and analysis are the customer's responsibility.
Priced per user per month, so cost scales with the number of people who need to build or read surveys rather than with portfolio size.

whyWeWin: A tool sends the survey; a program tells you what the number means. Kingsley gives the multifamily and CRE peer comparison SurveyMonkey structurally cannot.
Property, region and portfolio rollups arrive built; in SurveyMonkey somebody on your team builds and maintains them.
Residents, employees and commercial tenants in one benchmarked program instead of three disconnected survey files.
The finding routes into assigned training, a policy update and a mystery shop that verifies the fix.
askThis: When your SurveyMonkey results come back, what are you comparing the score to?
Who on your team owns writing the questions, chasing response rates and building the rollup — and what is that time worth?
Their benchmarks cover select Question Bank questions in English only. Does your resident base need Spanish?
How many seats would you need for everyone who has to read results, at $30 or $92 per user per month?
What happens between a bad survey result and someone actually changing behavior at the property?

objections.objection: We already have SurveyMonkey and it's cheap.
objections.response: It is, and for a one-off poll it's the right tool. The moment you need to know whether a 78 is good for a property like yours, you need a peer set — and per-seat pricing adds up fast once everyone who reads results needs a license.

objections.objection: They have benchmarks too.
objections.response: They do — on select Question Bank questions, English only, requiring 30+ organizations. There's no multifamily cut. That's the difference between a benchmark and a relevant benchmark.

doNotSay: Do not say SurveyMonkey has no benchmarks — Global and Industry Benchmarks are published products.
Do not quote a price other than the published figures ($30/user/month Team Advantage, $92/user/month Team Premier, annual billing, 3-user minimum).
Do not refer to the company as Momentive as though it were current — it reverted to the SurveyMonkey brand after the 2023 STG acquisition.
Do not claim SurveyMonkey is insecure or non-compliant without a named source.
Do not state a current headcount — not verified.

sv-resident.note: No resident survey product; a general-purpose builder the customer configures.

sv-employee.note: Employee survey templates and Question Bank content exist, but no managed employee engagement program.

sv-benchmark-dataset.note: Global Benchmarks (free with Question Bank questions) and paid Industry Benchmarks.

sv-benchmark-scale.note: Minimally disclosed. The only figure published is a threshold — a benchmark appears once "responses from 30+ organizations" exist. No total response count, no company count, no number of industries and no years of history are disclosed; benchmark data covers select Question Bank questions in English only. This is a finding: effective scale is Unknown.

sv-portfolio-rollup.note: No property/region/portfolio rollup; reporting is per-survey and must be assembled by the customer.

sv-lifecycle.note: Automation and triggering capabilities exist in higher tiers but a resident or employee lifecycle program is not offered as a product.

sv-custom-questions.note: Fully custom question authoring; note that benchmark comparison only applies to select Question Bank questions.

sv-investor-grade.note: No GRESB or real estate investor reporting.

sv-action-planning.note: No action-planning module in the published feature set; the product ends at analysis.

sv-published-pricing.note: Team Advantage $30/user/month; Team Premier $92/user/month; both billed annually with a 3-user minimum. Enterprise custom-quoted, 5-user minimum.
