name: Swift Bunny
toolCategory: Multifamily employee engagement and resident feedback platform

verdict.line: The only vendor we have found in this set that is multifamily-native on both the employee and resident side — compete strictly on benchmark scale, CRE tenant coverage and the ability to route a finding into training, policy and mystery shop verification, never on their industry credibility.

founded.value: Launched publicly June 2019 at NAA Apartmentalize

ownership.value: Private. Founded by Joe Bailey (founder and former CEO/President of Grace Hill); Doug Miller (founder of SatisFacts Research and ManagInc) is Chief Research Officer and partner; Jen Piccotti is President. No outside ownership or investment publicly disclosed as of Aug 2026.

size.value: Unknown — headcount not publicly disclosed

pricing.value: Not published. Site directs to a demo request; no pricing page or per-unit rate disclosed.

positioning.value: "Swift Bunny ONE" is positioned as an all-in-one employee retention platform for multifamily operators, built around Introduce (onboarding), Ingage (employee lifecycle feedback), Inquire (custom surveys) and Intouch (resident feedback), plus consultation and action planning.

strengths.text: Multifamily-native by design — the product is built only for rental housing operators, not adapted from a horizontal HR or survey tool.
Founding team carries deep multifamily lineage: Joe Bailey founded Grace Hill, and Doug Miller founded SatisFacts Research and ManagInc.

Covers both sides of the listening problem in one platform — Ingage for employee lifecycle feedback, Intouch for prospect and resident feedback — and explicitly links employee engagement to resident satisfaction.
Event-triggered lifecycle design on both sides: employee surveys fire at key moments in the employee lifecycle, resident/prospect feedback is solicited at key moments in the customer journey.
Intouch applies a proprietary algorithm across survey topic scores, importance and correlation with likelihood to renew to flag at-risk residents.
Publishes an annual Employee Engagement Risk Report and Employee Choice Awards, giving them recurring industry visibility.

gaps.text: Benchmark scale and history are not fully disclosed publicly. The Intouch page promises comparison to "rental housing peers" but discloses no respondent count, company count or years of history; the only public figure found is "over 6,500 multifamily employees nationwide last year" in the 2022 Employee Engagement Risk Report.
No commercial real estate tenant survey product appears in the published product line, which lists Introduce, Ingage, Inquire and Intouch only.
No pricing is published on the site — buyers cannot self-serve a cost comparison.

The published product line covers feedback, onboarding and action planning; it does not list a training/LMS, policy management or mystery shopping product, so a finding cannot be routed to verified remediation inside the same platform.

whyWeWin: Benchmark depth: the Kingsley Index™ carries decades of multifamily and commercial real estate benchmarking history; Swift Bunny does not publicly disclose comparable scale or history for its peer comparison.
CRE tenant coverage: Grace Hill surveys multifamily residents, employees and commercial tenants; Swift Bunny's published line is multifamily resident and employee only.

Closed loop: a Grace Hill survey finding routes into assigned training, a policy update and a mystery shop that verifies the behavior actually changed — Swift Bunny stops at insight and action planning.
One vendor, one contract across surveys, training, policy and shopping instead of stacking a feedback point solution on top of an LMS.
askThis: When your Swift Bunny report shows a peer comparison, how many responses and how many companies is that comparison built from, and over how many years?
Do you need to benchmark commercial tenants as well as residents? How does that work today?
When a survey surfaces a fair housing or service issue at one property, what happens next — who assigns the training, and how do you confirm the behavior actually changed?
Are you running a separate LMS and a separate policy system alongside this? What does that cost you in admin time and reconciliation?

objections.objection: Swift Bunny was built by people who actually know multifamily.
objections.response: Agreed, and we say so openly — Joe Bailey founded Grace Hill and Doug Miller founded SatisFacts. That is exactly why the comparison should be on scale and scope: the Kingsley Index™ brings decades of multifamily and CRE benchmarking history, and we can take a finding all the way through training, policy and a verification shop.

objections.objection: They do employee and resident feedback in one platform, same as you.
objections.response: They do — plus we add commercial tenant surveys, the Kingsley benchmark set, and the remediation path. Ask what happens on their side after the insight lands.

objections.objection: Their lifecycle triggers are more granular than an annual survey.
objections.response: Lifecycle and event-triggered surveys are table stakes for us too. The differentiator is what the number is compared against and what you can do about it inside the same system.

doNotSay: Never attack the industry credibility or multifamily experience of Swift Bunny's founders. Joe Bailey founded Grace Hill and Doug Miller founded SatisFacts Research — both facts are public and easily verified, and any 'they don't know multifamily' line will be disproven in the room and will cost you the deal. Compete only on benchmark scale, CRE tenant coverage and platform breadth.

Do not say 'Swift Bunny has no benchmark.' They publicly state Intouch compares a portfolio to rental housing peers. The accurate, defensible statement is that they do not publicly disclose the scale or history of that benchmark.
Do not say they are a startup or unproven — they have been shipping since 2019 and publish annual industry research.
Do not quote a Swift Bunny price, headcount, client count or benchmark size. None of these are publicly disclosed.
Do not claim they cannot do employee surveys well — employee lifecycle feedback is their founding product.
Do not imply any Grace Hill relationship, endorsement or shared data because of the founder history. There is none.

sv-resident.note: Intouch collects prospect and resident feedback at key moments in the customer journey.

sv-employee.note: Ingage is the employee lifecycle feedback system; it was the founding product.

sv-cre-tenant.note: No commercial tenant survey product is listed in the published product line; no public statement either way.

sv-benchmark-dataset.note: "Compare your portfolio's results to your rental housing peers, providing industry-specific performance insights."

sv-benchmark-scale.note: Scale largely undisclosed. Only public figure found: "over 6,500 multifamily employees nationwide last year" completed engagement surveys (2022 Employee Engagement Risk Report). No company count, no resident-side respondent count, and no years-of-history statement is published. Treat overall scale as Unknown.

sv-portfolio-rollup.note: Dashboard allows drill-down "by region, community, or individual responses."

sv-lifecycle.note: Employee surveys triggered at key lifecycle moments; resident/prospect feedback solicited automatically at key journey moments.

sv-custom-questions.note: Inquire is a custom survey builder sold alongside the benchmarked core products.

sv-sentiment.note: Open-text analysis is not described on the public product pages.

sv-investor-grade.note: No GRESB or investor reporting claim found on public pages.

sv-action-planning.note: "Consultation & Action Planning" is a named part of the Swift Bunny ONE suite.

sv-published-pricing.note: No pricing page or published rate on swiftbunny.com; site routes to demo request.

name: The Fair Housing Institute
toolCategory: Single-topic compliance training specialist — attorney-written fair housing courses sold per course or licensed onto a client's own platform

verdict.line: A credible, attorney-authored point solution that wins the fair housing course on price and depth but leaves the buyer without a training system — compete on the whole program, never on the single course.

hq.value: 7742 Spalding Dr., Suite 478, Peachtree Corners, GA

ownership.value: Private (The Fair Housing Institute, Inc.); Kathelene Williams named as founder

pricing.value: Published per course. Basics of Fair Housing Certification $99 (3.5 hrs); Fair Housing in a Flash $79 (1 hr); Maintenance Professionals $79; Single Family Rentals $99; Advanced Fair Housing $119 (2 hrs); Fair Housing and Seniors $59; Fair Housing and Student Living $59; Housing Choice Voucher programs $149; micro-learning courses $39–$49. Group accounts available; group pricing not published.

positioning.value: "Fair housing training at the click of a button" — on-demand, interactive courses created by fair housing attorneys.

strengths.text: Attorney-created content, positioned on legal authorship rather than instructional design.
Deep segment-specific fair housing coverage: seniors, student living, single family rentals, Housing Choice Voucher programs, maintenance professionals.
Micro-learning library on high-liability edge cases — hoarding, VAWA/domestic violence, assistance animals, criminal history screening, harassment, live-in aides, marketing.
TDHCA and Virginia DPOR approved, with certification exams and certificates of completion.
English and Spanish available.
Transparent published per-course pricing ($39–$149), which lowers the barrier to a departmental purchase without procurement.
Offers a 'train on your platform' licensing model so clients can host the content on their own LMS.

gaps.text: Scope is fair housing only — the published catalog contains no leasing, maintenance, safety, harassment-beyond-fair-housing, customer service or operations curriculum.
The course catalog page does not describe SCORM export, mobile-specific access, CEC credits beyond the named state approvals, or custom authoring services.
No role- or property-based automatic assignment, compliance dashboard, PMS integration or HRIS integration is described in public materials.
Published state approvals are Texas (TDHCA) and Virginia (DPOR) only.

whyWeWin: Fair housing is one course in a program, not the program — ask what covers maintenance safety, harassment, leasing skills and onboarding.
Per-seat course purchases don't scale into portfolio-wide assignment, tracking and audit reporting; a growing operator outgrows the model.
No published role-based assignment means someone is manually deciding who takes what, every time there's turnover.
Grace Hill connects fair housing training to mystery shop evidence — you can see whether the behavior actually changed on site.
askThis: Beyond fair housing, what covers maintenance safety, harassment and leasing skills for this team?
When someone new starts at a property, who assigns their courses and how do they know it happened?
If you're audited, can you produce completion by property, by role, by date — or is it a spreadsheet?
How does per-course pricing behave as you grow from a few hundred to a few thousand employees?
For the states beyond Texas and Virginia in your portfolio, what covers the jurisdiction-specific requirements?

objections.objection: Their content is written by fair housing attorneys.
objections.response: That's a real strength — say so. The question is whether one excellent course is a training program: who assigns it, who tracks it, and what covers everything else on the risk list.

objections.objection: It's $99 a person, you're much more expensive.
objections.response: That's a per-course price for one topic. Compare it to a full program across every role and every risk area, with assignment, tracking and audit reporting included — the unit isn't the same.

objections.objection: We already use FHI and it works.
objections.response: Then keep the thing that works and look at what's uncovered. Most operators using a single-topic vendor have no system of record for everything else.

doNotSay: Their content isn't credible — it is attorney-authored and state-approved.
They don't have Spanish — English and Spanish are published as available.
They can't integrate with an LMS — they offer a 'train on your platform' licensing option.
Any claim about FHI's founding year, size, ownership or customer count — none is published.

name: The Status Quo — shared drive, binder, and email acknowledgments
aka: The binder in the leasing office
Word docs on the S: drive
toolCategory: No system — shared drive, printed binder, and email or paper sign-off

verdict.line: The most common competitor and the hardest to beat — it costs nothing, works well enough on a normal Tuesday, and fails only on the day it matters most.

pricing.value: No subscription cost. The real cost is staff time to write and maintain policies, plus unquantified risk exposure — neither of which appears on any budget line.

positioning.value: "We already have policies. They're on the shared drive."

strengths.text: Zero subscription cost. There is no line item, no renewal, no procurement cycle, and no budget conversation to lose. For an operator watching every dollar, this is a genuinely rational default.
Simple and universally understood. Everyone knows how to open a Word document, print a page, and reply 'received' to an email. There is no adoption curve and no change management project.
No training required. Nobody has to learn a new system, remember a new login, or sit through an onboarding webinar. Onsite teams already have enough software to log into.
Total control and total flexibility. The policies say exactly what leadership wants them to say, in the company's own voice, and can be changed in thirty seconds by anyone with edit access.
It has worked so far. Most operators running this way have never had an incident where it failed, which makes the risk feel theoretical and the spend feel unnecessary.

gaps.text: Nobody owns regulatory currency. Policies are updated when someone remembers or when something goes wrong, so the manual drifts further from current fair housing and housing compliance guidance every year it sits untouched.

No single current version. Copies proliferate across property folders, laptops, printed binders and email attachments, and there is no way to know which properties are working from an outdated manual.

Acknowledgment evidence is not defensible. An email reply saying 'got it' does not establish which version of which policy the employee received, and reconstructing that trail after a complaint means searching mailboxes of people who may no longer work there.
No overdue visibility. There is no way to answer 'which employees at which properties have not acknowledged the current policy' without someone building a spreadsheet by hand.
New hires and transfers fall through. Onboarding acknowledgment depends on an individual manager remembering to send the file, which fails silently and is invisible until an audit.
Policy and training are disconnected. There is no way to show that the person who acknowledged the fair housing policy also completed the fair housing course.
The hidden labor cost is real but invisible. Someone on staff writes and rewrites this content, and that cost never shows up next to the zero on the subscription line.

whyWeWin: The buyer's real problem is not storage — it is authorship. Grace Hill ships over a thousand customizable multifamily policies, forms and job descriptions across 18+ manuals, written by multifamily experts, covering emergency procedures, leasing, tax credit compliance, maintenance and operations. The status quo supplies a folder; we supply the content.

Grace Hill owns keeping the content current as multifamily regulation changes. In the status quo, that job belongs to a person who already has a full-time job, which is why the manual is three years old.

Secure electronic acknowledgments create a digital paper trail tying a named employee to a specific policy version on a specific date — the artifact counsel asks for, produced in seconds instead of reconstructed from email.
Automatic assignment by location, position, group or employee means new hires and transfers get the right policies without a manager remembering to send anything.
Policies and training live together in PerformanceHQ, so the acknowledgment and the course that teaches the behavior report as one story.
askThis: When was your policy manual last updated, and who did it?
If a fair housing complaint landed tomorrow, how long would it take you to prove this employee acknowledged this version of that policy on a specific date — and where would you look?
How many of your properties are working from a copy that is no longer current? How would you find out?
Who acknowledged the last policy update, and who didn't? Can you pull that in the next five minutes?
When you hired someone last month, what guaranteed they received and acknowledged the current policies?
How many hours a year does your compliance or ops person spend rewriting policy language — and what would they do with that time instead?
When a leasing consultant has a policy question at 4pm on a Friday, what do they actually do?

objections.objection: We already have policies. They're on the shared drive.
objections.response: I believe you — almost everyone does. Two questions though. When were they last updated for current fair housing guidance, and if a complaint came in tomorrow, could you produce proof that a specific employee acknowledged a specific version on a specific date? Those are the two moments the shared drive can't cover.

objections.objection: This has worked fine for us for years.
objections.response: That's usually true right up until it isn't. The shared drive works every day except the one day you need evidence. We're not selling you insurance against a hypothetical — we're selling you back the hours your team spends writing policy language, plus a record you can actually produce.

objections.objection: We can't justify the cost when what we have is free.
objections.response: It isn't free — it's unbilled. Somebody on your payroll writes and rewrites those manuals, and that time is real money that just never gets counted. Add up those hours, then compare. And that's before you price a single hour of counsel's time reconstructing an acknowledgment trail from email.

objections.objection: Our attorney reviewed our handbook last year.
objections.response: That's more than most operators do. Was it your operations manuals too — fair housing procedures, leasing, tax credit files, emergency response? And what is the plan for keeping them current between reviews? A one-time review is a snapshot; regulation keeps moving.

doNotSay: Do not tell a prospect their current approach is negligent, reckless, or that they are exposed to lawsuits. It insults the person you are selling to, and it is a legal characterization we are not qualified to make.

Do not invent or cite a statistic about fair housing settlement amounts, litigation frequency, or the cost of non-compliance. If we do not have an approved sourced figure, use the customer's own numbers instead.
Do not claim Grace Hill Policies eliminates legal risk or guarantees compliance. We supply content and evidence; we do not provide legal advice.
Do not mock the binder. Many buyers built it themselves and are proud of it. Respect the effort, then show what it cannot do.

toolCategory: Spaced-repetition microlearning reinforcement app — short daily drills on top of training someone else supplies

verdict.line: A knowledge-retention layer, not a training system — no multifamily content and no published compliance coverage, so it reinforces what a buyer already has rather than replacing it.

pricing.value: Not published.

positioning.value: Positions itself around helping organizations "ditch dull training and build learning habits that drive real results" using spaced repetition — a learning technique for long-term knowledge retention — delivered as roughly two-minute daily drills.

strengths.text: Built entirely on spaced repetition for long-term knowledge retention — a defensible pedagogical differentiator most LMS vendors do not claim.
Extremely low time cost per learner — daily drills of roughly two minutes, which suits high-turnover frontline teams.
AI Content Builder rapidly generates quizzes from a customer's existing materials.
Established since 2014 with named enterprise clients including The North Face, DFIN, Renault and Cunard.
Analytics and performance reporting on knowledge retention over time, not just completion.

gaps.text: Named industries served are retail, utilities and hospitality; multifamily and property management are not mentioned and no multifamily client is named.
The About page does not describe a vendor-supplied course library — the content model is built around a customer's existing materials via the AI Content Builder.
The About page does not specify mobile app details, offline functionality, SCORM compliance, language support, integrations or pricing.
No fair housing, state-specific compliance or CEC/credential content is described.
UK-headquartered with no published US multifamily presence or US regulatory content.

whyWeWin: Wranx reinforces knowledge someone else created — it does not supply fair housing, state compliance or multifamily role content.
Two-minute quizzes are a retention mechanism, not a compliance record; ask what an auditor would accept.
No published US multifamily clients or US regulatory content, and the company is UK-based.
If a prospect likes the retention idea, position Grace Hill's competency assessment as the same instinct applied to content that already exists and is maintained.
askThis: Where would the fair housing content come from — Wranx builds quizzes from material you already have.
Do you have a US multifamily reference we can speak with?

Does it work offline for maintenance techs who lose signal in a basement?

objections.objection: Spaced repetition actually makes training stick — that's better than another LMS.
objections.response: The learning science is real and worth respecting. It's a reinforcement layer though: it needs source content, and for multifamily that content is the expensive, regulated part.

objections.objection: It's two minutes a day, our teams will actually do it.
objections.response: Engagement is a genuine strength. The question to settle first is whether daily quizzes satisfy your compliance obligation — usually you'll need both.

They have no content at all — the About page doesn't describe a course library, which is not the same as confirming none exists.

name: Xoralia
toolCategory: Policy management app for Microsoft 365 and SharePoint

verdict.line: A focused, well-built attestation layer for buyers committed to Microsoft 365 — it solves the acknowledgment problem SharePoint cannot, and does nothing about what the policy says.

hq.value: Not published on the vendor site; Content Formula Limited is a UK-based Microsoft Certified Partner.

founded.value: Not published on the vendor site

ownership.value: Built and owned by Content Formula Limited, a Microsoft Certified Partner.

size.value: Vendor states 427,000 active users across its customer base.

pricing.value: Not published. A free trial is offered and buyers are directed to contact sales for a quote.

positioning.value: Positions itself as a policy management platform operating natively within Microsoft 365, automating the full policy lifecycle from creation through distribution, acknowledgment and audit documentation, with deployment "measured in days, not months."

strengths.text: Native Microsoft 365 delivery — policies distributed through Teams and SharePoint with no separate login, which removes the single biggest adoption barrier for a standalone policy tool.
Solves exactly what plain SharePoint cannot: automated acknowledgment capture, timestamped audit trails, and escalation for overdue actions.
Audience targeting delivers policies by role using Entra ID integration, plus a centralized policy library with version control.
Automated review cycles that trigger on schedule, addressing policy staleness at the process level.
Vendor reports an average attestation rate of 84% and 427,000 active users; free trial available before purchase.

gaps.text: Xoralia's site describes lifecycle automation, distribution and acknowledgment; it does not describe a prewritten policy content library of any kind, and no multifamily content is described.
Vendor-maintained regulatory updates to policy text and jurisdiction-specific policy variants are not described on the vendor site.
Named target markets are financial services, healthcare, education, charities, government/public sector, energy, manufacturing and construction. Multifamily housing is not among them.
Pricing is not published.

whyWeWin: Xoralia proves the acknowledgment was captured. Grace Hill supplies what was acknowledged — over a thousand multifamily policies, forms and job descriptions across 18+ manuals, written by multifamily experts.

Xoralia's automated review cycle reminds your team that a policy is due for review. Grace Hill does the reviewing and updating for multifamily regulation, so the reminder does not land on a person who has no time to act on it.
Grace Hill links policy to multifamily training in one platform — the fair housing policy and the fair housing course report together.
Grace Hill assigns by location, position, group or employee — properties and regions, not just Entra ID groups an admin has to build and maintain.
askThis: Xoralia automates the reminder that a policy needs review. Who does the actual rewriting, and how long do those reminders sit unactioned today?
Does Xoralia supply any policy text, or is it purely the distribution and acknowledgment layer?
Does search reach inside your policy documents, or is it a policy library index — and if the former, is that SharePoint's search or Xoralia's?
How many multifamily operators do they have, and can you speak to one?
Do your onsite maintenance techs live in Teams, or would this only reach your corporate staff?

objections.objection: Xoralia sits inside Teams and SharePoint so adoption will be easy, and it's probably cheaper.
objections.response: The native delivery is a real advantage and we won't dismiss it. But notice the scope: it moves and tracks documents. Nobody at Xoralia is writing your fair housing policy or updating it when a rule changes. You would be buying better plumbing for content you still have to produce and maintain yourself.

objections.objection: They already handle attestation and review cycles.
objections.response: They do, and that's genuinely better than raw SharePoint. Ask a follow-up though: when the review reminder fires, who rewrites the policy? If the answer is 'our compliance team, when they get to it,' the reminder is not the bottleneck — the writing is.

doNotSay: Do not claim Xoralia lacks attestation, version control, audience targeting or overdue escalation — all are documented on their site.
Do not assert Xoralia has 'no content library' as an absolute. Say it is not described on their site and ask the question.
Do not repeat Xoralia's 84% attestation rate or 427,000 user figure as an independently verified benchmark — they are vendor-reported.
Do not quote a price.

name: Yardi Aspire
toolCategory: Learning management system built by a property management software vendor, sold with its own real estate course library

verdict.line: The most credible head-to-head LMS in the category — it has real multifamily content, state-approved fair housing, 100+ Spanish courses and AI authoring, so win on outcome proof (competency, shops, surveys, benchmarks) rather than on feature checklists.

ownership.value: Private

size.value: Over 9,000 professionals in more than 40 offices worldwide (company-wide, not Aspire-specific)

pricing.value: Not published. Three named tiers exist — Aspire, Aspire Plus and Aspire Platinum.

positioning.value: Positions Aspire as an advanced online learning tool that centralizes training, policies and resources in a single mobile-friendly hub to activate employee potential across onboarding, compliance and performance.

strengths.text: State-approved fair housing content: fair housing courses approved by TDHCA and the Florida DBPR that qualify for continuing education credit.
State-variant harassment prevention course pages for California, Connecticut, New York, Maine and Illinois, with stated ongoing regulatory updates.
More than 100 bilingual English/Spanish courses plus Canadian French options.
AI content-generation tooling that builds interactive courses, scenario challenges, assessments and translations inside the authoring environment.
Single sign-on across the Yardi ecosystem via YardiOne, making it low-friction for existing Voyager clients.
Supports NAA credential maintenance (CAM, CAPS, CALP).

gaps.text: Capability is split across three purchase tiers — SCORM compatibility, embedded e-signature, live polling and Microsoft Teams integration are named as Platinum-tier features, so the base tier is not the same product.
No benchmarking of training performance against an industry dataset is described on the Aspire product page or the published course catalog overview.
The published catalog does not state a total course count, so library depth cannot be compared line-for-line from public sources.
Fair housing state approvals named publicly are Texas (TDHCA) and Florida (DBPR); no broader multi-state fair housing approval list is published.

whyWeWin: Grace Hill measures competency, not just completion — tie the conversation to what the team can demonstrate, not what they clicked through.
Aspire proves training happened; PerformanceHQ connects training to mystery shop scores, resident and employee survey results and reputation signals in one place.
Aspire's published fair housing state approvals are Texas and Florida — for a multi-state portfolio, ask how each additional jurisdiction is covered.
Capability is tiered (Aspire / Plus / Platinum) — confirm which tier the quoted price actually buys before comparing features.
askThis: Which Aspire tier is in the quote — base, Plus or Platinum? Which of the features you were shown are Platinum-only?
For the states your portfolio operates in beyond Texas and Florida, what fair housing approval or jurisdiction variant is provided?
How do you know a leasing consultant can actually do the thing, versus that they finished the course?
How would you compare your training completion against what the rest of the industry is doing?
If your organization moves off Yardi Voyager, what happens to the training system and the completion history?

objections.objection: It's already in our Yardi stack, so it's simpler.
objections.response: Single sign-on is real and worth something. The question is what the content does after login — ask which tier you're on, which states are covered, and whether you can show competency rather than completion.

objections.objection: Yardi has AI course creation now.
objections.response: Authoring speed is a content-production feature. Our value is the content already being written, maintained and jurisdiction-current, plus the ability to connect what people learned to what happened at the property.

objections.objection: Yardi has Spanish content too.
objections.response: Agreed — that's a genuine strength on their side. Take the comparison to depth and currency: which courses are bilingual, and who updates them when regulation changes.

doNotSay: They don't have fair housing content — they do, with published Texas and Florida approvals.
They don't have Spanish content — they publish 100+ bilingual courses.
They can't do SCORM — SCORM compatibility is named in the Platinum tier.
Any claim about Aspire's price, customer count or course count — none is published.

tr-multifamily-content.note: Catalog includes an Industry Training category of foundational real estate courses alongside Yardi software, compliance, safety and leadership categories.

verdict.line: Research-house data on a monthly survey rhythm, sold to investment and research buyers — compete on refresh cadence and on who inside the organization actually needs the number.

strengths.text: Broad market coverage: the site cites 224 markets, with references elsewhere to 183 U.S. markets and 'more than 150 markets'.

whyWeWin: For a pricing or leasing decision made this week, a monthly stratified survey is a different instrument than a daily unit-level feed — make the buyer name the decision cadence.

name: Zavanta by COMPROSE
toolCategory: Policy and procedure authoring and governance platform

verdict.line: A serious structured-authoring tool for regulated industries — it makes writing policies easier, but the buyer is still the author, and multifamily is not a market it names.

hq.value: Not published on the vendor site

founded.value: Not published on the vendor site

ownership.value: Acquired by Volaris Group, announced March 18, 2026.

size.value: Not published

pricing.value: Not published. Prospects are directed to request a demo or download a buyer's guide.

positioning.value: "Zavanta helps high-stakes organizations govern policies, procedures, approvals, and records to prevent risk, prove control, and respond with evidence." Explicitly positions itself as more than a document repository.

strengths.text: Structured authoring with reusable templates — genuinely better than a Word-and-folder approach for organizations that must write a lot of procedure content consistently.
Read/Verify, e-signature and attestation tracking with audit trails, ownership records and attestation history designed to satisfy auditors and regulators.
Full-text searchable guidance and role-aware content delivery, so staff see the procedures relevant to their role.
Test and quiz generation tied directly to procedures — comprehension checking built into the policy layer.
Now part of Volaris Group, a long-hold acquirer, which typically means product continuity rather than sunset risk.

gaps.text: Zavanta names its target markets as banking, credit unions, healthcare, manufacturing and multi-site operations. Multifamily housing is not among them.
The product provides structured authoring templates — a way to write content — and does not describe a prewritten library of written multifamily policy content.
A vendor-maintained regulatory update service for policy content is not described on the product site.
Pricing is not published.

whyWeWin: Zavanta makes authoring efficient. Grace Hill makes authoring unnecessary — over a thousand multifamily policies, forms and job descriptions across 18+ manuals arrive already written by multifamily experts.

Grace Hill keeps the content current against multifamily regulatory change as part of the subscription; a structured authoring tool hands that responsibility back to the buyer no matter how good its templates are.
Our policy library links directly to multifamily training in PerformanceHQ, written by the same subject matter experts — quiz generation is not the same thing as a fair housing course.
Assignment maps to properties, regions and onsite positions, which is how a multifamily org chart is actually shaped.
askThis: Their templates give you a structure. Who fills it in with your fair housing, leasing and tax-credit language, and how many hours is that?
When a regulation changes, does Zavanta revise your policy text, or just make it easier for your team to revise it?
How many multifamily operators are on their reference list?
What does implementation look like — do they migrate your existing manuals and restructure them, or is that your team's work?
Now that COMPROSE is inside Volaris, who owns your account and what has been committed on roadmap?

objections.objection: Zavanta's structured authoring will make our writing much faster.
objections.response: It probably will, and that's a real benefit if you're committed to writing your own. The question is whether you want to be in the policy-writing business at all. We hand you over a thousand multifamily policies already written, and we keep them current. Faster authoring is still authoring.

objections.objection: They serve heavily regulated industries, so they understand compliance.
objections.response: They do — banking, credit unions, healthcare. That expertise is in the governance mechanics, not in your regulations. Their public material does not describe monitoring HUD guidance or state landlord-tenant law. That is the part Grace Hill maintains.

doNotSay: Do not say Zavanta is just a document repository — the vendor explicitly positions against that and it would read as uninformed.
Do not claim Zavanta lacks attestation or search — it markets Read/Verify, e-signature, attestation tracking and full-text searchable guidance.
Do not speculate about what the Volaris acquisition means for the product or support — say only what the press release says.
Do not quote a price.
